title_original: Jordan Firstman : « J’ai fait mon coming out à 12 ans. C’est jeune, mais je n’ai jamais pu garder quelque chose pour moi. »
editorial_title_zh: 乔丹·费斯特曼：“我12岁就出柜了。年纪是小了点，但我这人从来藏不住话。”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 11月4日，演员、编剧兼网红乔丹·费斯特曼将推出他的首部长片电影——兼具美感与凝聚力的《俱乐部小孩》。在2023年通过塞巴斯蒂安·席尔瓦疯狂的《日光腐烂》认识他之后，我们曾向他询问那些与其身份产生共鸣的最初影像……

article_text:
“ La première image, c’était dans l’émission The Real World. Philadelphia [l’équivalent de Loft Story ; la saison en question a été diffusée de septembre 2004 à mars 2005 sur MTV, ndlr]. Il y avait notamment un personnage gay nommé Willie. Dans un épisode, il ramène un mec dans la maison, et ils sont filmés en train de prendre une douche ensemble, ils se shampouinent les cheveux. C’était de loin le truc le plus érotique que j’avais vu de ma vie. J’ai fait mon coming out à 12 ans. J’ai dit que j’étais gay à tout mon entourage trois jours après l’avoir compris.

« Club Kid » de Jordan Firstman : un récit d’apprentissage queer et crépusculaire

C’est jeune, mais je n’ai jamais réussi à garder quelque chose pour moi – je crois que c’est assez clair maintenant, étant donné la manière dont je m’expose sur les réseaux. Je suis né en 1991, avant l’arrivée d’Internet, mais j’y ai eu accès à partir de l’âge de 10 ou 11 ans. Ça m’a permis de voir du porno en cliquant sur les petites fenêtres qui s’affichaient dans les coins et en patientant pendant le temps hyper long du téléchargement. J’ai l’impression que la plupart des hommes gays ont une obsession pour les icônes féminines, ce qui n’est pas trop mon cas. J’ai toujours été plus intéressé par les hommes et par le sexe avec eux.

Vers 14 ans, je faisais du théâtre communautaire, et je me suis fait une amie, Alana, qui m’a fait découvrir la série Queer as Folk, dans sa version originale. Elle planquait des versions piratées de DVD chez ses parents. J’ai regardé des épisodes et ça m’a semblé dingue, je n’avais aucune idée de ce à quoi ressemblait la vie gay.

Ah ! J’étais aussi obsédé par Stephen Sondheim, le metteur en scène de comédies musicales. Mes potes et moi, on était vraiment des loseurs, on s’échangeait des potins sur lui. J’avais entendu dire qu’il avait un donjon du sexe dans la cave de son appart à New York. Un vrai pervers. J’ai longtemps cherché à changer la représentation des gays à travers mon travail. À la base, je ne faisais ça que pour nous, je ne me suis jamais senti en mission de « normaliser » l’homosexualité pour les hétéros. Ils pensent ce qu’ils pensent. Même si l’homophobie est encore très répandue et vivace, je ne serai jamais quelqu’un qui va se battre pour les droits LGBTQ+, même si c’est hyper important. Il y a des gens bien meilleurs que moi pour faire ça. Je me suis donc toujours plutôt adressé aux gays.”

Club Kid de Jordan Firstman, Metropolitan FilmExport (2 h 02), sortie le 4 novembre

excerpt_original: Le 4 novembre, l’acteur, scénariste et influenceur sortira son premier long métrage, le beau et fédérateur "Club Kid". En le découvrant en 2023 dans le survolté Rotting in the Sun de Sebastián Silva, on l’avait interrogé sur les premières images qui ont résonné avec son identité…

title_original: Lunch With Adam: Met Curator Alisa LaGamma on Repatriation, the Revitalized Rockefeller Wing, the Benin Bronzes, and More
editorial_title_zh: 与 Adam 共进午餐：专访策展人 Alisa LaGamma，谈文物归还、焕新的 Rockefeller 展翼、贝宁青铜器等议题
editorial_excerpt_zh: “今后我们都需要想出富有创意的解决方案。”

Pulitzer 策展人。我毕生收藏非洲艺术，多年来看过她策划的许多展览，也曾多年担任该部门委员会成员，近年还任过主席。这些物件的历史引人入胜：从痛苦的殖民时代，到人们努力让艺术界广泛接纳这些艺术。很少有人意识到，大都会直到 20 世纪 80 年代才展出这些作品；在那之前，许多人眼里它们不过是文物。如今，围绕归还政治及遣返复杂现实的讨论仍在持续。上个月我们从巴黎的经典非洲与大洋洲艺术博览会 Parcours du Monde 归来；此前不久，博物馆整座展翼耗资 7000 万美元翻修一周年。此时探讨当下热议的几个议题，正合时宜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：Michael C. Rockefeller 展翼是什么？能否介绍大都会与经典非洲、大洋洲和古代美洲艺术之间的关系？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：当然，这是个引人入胜的故事。1969 年，纽约州州长 Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller 与大都会艺术博物馆宣布将兴建一座新展翼，以接收他捐赠的撒哈拉以南非洲、大洋洲和古代美洲藏品。在此之前，这批藏品一直陈列于他创办的原始艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一发展从根本上重塑了大都会的使命。当时的大都会——如今亦然——是美国的顶尖博物馆之一。此举让占世界艺术传统约四分之三的艺术，突然得以与西欧艺术史巅峰——西方古典大师作品——并列受到认可；此前，这些传统常被归入自然历史博物馆。几乎一夜之间，大都会成为一家全球性机构，立志呈现所有文化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这在当时是相当激进的一步——一次重大转变，改变了西方人看待世界广大地区艺术的方式，也对收藏家、画廊和博物馆产生了深远影响，拓宽了人们对何为美术的理解。但人们或许不知道，大都会起初并不支持这件事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：确实如此。Rockefeller 推动的这场转型来之不易。他对非西方艺术的热情起初并未得到大都会认同，因此他在 1954 年于现代艺术博物馆对面创办了自己的私人机构。当时艺术史中这些领域尚十分新兴，他在相关顶尖专家的建议下，着手梳理大都会尚未涵盖的主要艺术传统。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/TWO-PANEL-SPLIT-WITH-BACKGROUND-2-1024x819.png", "alt": "Alisa LaGamma 与 Adam Lindemann 的双人照片。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma 与 Adam Lindemann。照片：大都会艺术博物馆及作者提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这位政治家出身于美国最富有的家族之一，可以说是美国最接近王室的人物；他却希望把那些被视为来自世界边远地区的民族志材料的物件，当作美术来认可。他为何如此热衷？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：Nelson 于 1930 年从达特茅斯学院毕业，那一年便成为大都会的受托人。作为 John D. Rockefeller 与 Abby Rockefeller 之子，他从母亲那里受到影响，认识到非洲和古代美洲艺术在 20 世纪艺术转型中发挥的重要作用。此后，他以国际主义者和政治家的身份，通过艺术传统学习较少为人熟悉的地区，并由此坚信“所有人都有艺术”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nelson 的儿子 Michael 也怀有父亲那份使命感，并在哈佛主修人类学。他深受太平洋地区的文化与艺术启发，旅居当地期间也以新的方式探究艺术实践。展翼中展出的 Asmat 雕塑极为醒目，是他在新几内亚西南部研究并收藏的。1961 年，他第二次前往巴布亚新几内亚，研究、收藏并记录当地艺术家的作品；途中，他乘坐的小船在 Betsj 河口燃料耗尽，漂向阿拉弗拉海。他试图游向岸边时不幸溺亡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这一切发生在 20 世纪 60 至 70 年代，当时包括美国在内的许多地区都经历着文化与社会的重大变革。这些变化如何影响了相关藏品进入大都会？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：20 世纪 60 展翼更新工程。我的策展团队希望重新构想博物馆的这一部分，并以三组独立的世界艺术概览重新呈现常设藏品：既以历史为基础，也纳入多层次内容，并通过与来源国专家交流而丰富起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：Alisa，你在大都会艺术博物馆工作多久了？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我还是研究生时就来到博物馆，至今约 31 年。过去 12 年里，我负责 Michael C. Rockefeller 展翼，并组建专家团队照料藏品所涉及的三个地区的艺术。此前，我只是一名资深非洲艺术专家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：你出生在非洲。你的成长经历如何影响你研究非洲艺术的兴趣？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我父亲是美国外交官，职业生涯在非洲和欧洲度过。他深爱自己在撒哈拉以南非洲工作过的许多地方。我出生于刚果民主共和国卢本巴希，成长关键时期在赞比亚、科特迪瓦和多哥度过。我读大学和研究生期间，家人住在塞内加尔、尼日利亚和南非；那也是我逐渐把关注点转向艺术史和非洲艺术的时期。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：最近，我们和一群大都会的朋友一同参加了巴黎一年一度的非洲与大洋洲艺术博览会 Parcours du Monde（“环游世界”）。在那里我们看了所有参展商，也去了卢浮宫的“五大洲”展翼以及布朗利河岸博物馆的世界艺术展。我觉得此行最有意思、也最发人深省的一站，是布鲁塞尔特尔菲伦的比利时皇家中非博物馆。我从 20 多岁后期起就一直喜欢非洲艺术，也读过 Adam Hochschild 写的《利奥波德国王的鬼魂》，了解比利时暴力的殖民历史。不过，直到那时我才突然意识到，如今已是 2026 年，他们仍然占有数千件物品——这些东西是在当地被称为“刚果自由邦”时期由利奥波德二世国王的私人武装夺走或盗取的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：特尔菲伦是欧洲殖民势力在非洲存在的独特遗迹，也是那段历史中最黑暗的篇章之一。这个机构基本上是为展示中非广袤领土的财富和丰富自然资源而建立的；比利时国王利奥波德曾宣称对这片土地拥有主权。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这是哪一年？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：1800 年代末，具体说是 1898 年，在 1897 年布鲁塞尔国际博览会举办临时殖民展之后。它是利奥波德宣传机器的一部分。它不是艺术博物馆，也从未被设想为艺术博物馆。它真正展示的是矿产、木材、野生动物，以及那里资源的惊人财富。特尔菲伦的文物反映了比利时人在该地区数十年的存在。其中许多是比利时人在服役期满后带回的物品，随后卖给特尔菲伦或作为礼物转交。许多不同的人从刚果回来：有传教士，也有参加过军事行动的人；有些人纯粹是行政官员。因此，这批文物汇集了比利时人在该地区长期活动的痕迹，也记录了比利时人与中非当地居民之间不同的互动。有些互动极为暴力残酷，有些则相对温和，但这段历史尤其令人创伤。Joseph Conrad 曾亲历刚果自由邦建立初期，他把所见写进《黑暗之心》，有力批判了欧洲殖民主义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Commemorative-portrait_Edo-812x1024.jpg", "alt": "一件埃多人的纪念肖像作品。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ùhúnmwèlaò（纪念肖像），约 16 世纪作品，由 Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n（青铜铸造行会）为埃多人创作；由尼日利亚国家博物馆委员会借展给大都会艺术博物馆。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：我们看到那件令人惊叹的刚果权力像，上面缠着许多绶带，面容也十分摄人。它是一件非凡杰作，背后还有一段故事。军事掠夺者 Alexandre Delcommune 因货物经过当地时欠缴关税而袭击首领 Ne Kuko。争端涉及通行费的收取金额。当地人的神圣护符被没收了。Ne Kuko 想要拿回来，Delcommune 拒绝归还，最后它落入特尔菲伦手中。他夺走了他们的神像，可为什么把它交给特尔菲伦？为什么不自己留下？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：他是个不受监管的商人，面对即将出台、并向他征收的关税，便自行其是。他对此愤怒不已，想要仗势压人。他曾在当地生活，知道那件物品确有力量，也知道它在案件仲裁和裁决中发挥着重要的心理作用；夺走它，是削弱地方官员权威的极端手段。我无法想象那样的人会在意把这件作品留在自己手里。对他而言，重要的是把它夺走。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "特尔菲伦这样的机构有一种讽刺之处：我们保存着这些故事，详细记录了特定作品在原生社群中发挥的作用。我们对这件雕塑被移走之前的身份了解很多；这本身就是极其重要的历史文献。这件作品在视觉上令人叹为观止，同时也是一场冲突的物质见证。因此，特尔菲伦的藏品能让我们学到许多。它们是非常珍贵的记录，不该被埋没。相关材料理应更广泛地向公众开放，让我们更深入理解历史上发生的一切。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这就引出了显而易见的问题：接下来会怎样？博物馆该如何处置这些藏品？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：这正是来源研究以及与相关同行和社群持续对话至关重要的地方。大都会长期将这类研究纳入策展实践，相关领域的专业能力已积累逾 25 年。并非每件物品或每批藏品都适用同一个答案。比利时已就现有国有藏品通过立法，并正与刚果民主共和国积极讨论文化遗产与归还问题；这些讨论引出了更广泛的问题，包括公众如何接触作品、如何保护、如何研究，以及在哪里才能最有意义地欣赏作品。关键在于调查并公开这些历史，并让与相关物件联系最密切的机构和社群参与决定下一步。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Queen-Mother_Edo-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "一件埃多人王母像。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Iyọ́bà（王母像），约 18 世纪作品，由 Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n（青铜铸造行会）为埃多人创作；由尼日利亚国家博物馆委员会借展给大都会艺术博物馆。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：简单说一句“全部送回去”，并不能涵盖其中的复杂性与现实情况。你谈的是一个幅员辽阔的国家、不同的社群、不同的历史，以及数以千计各不相同的物件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：这些问题需要通过合作逐一厘清，而不是抽象地给出答案。在这个过程中，我们不应忽略作品本身作为文化成就的重要性；我们应该尊重并珍视这些成就。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从某种意义上说，这又让我们回到刚才谈的 Rockefeller 展翼。博物馆继承了特定历史时期形成的收藏、分类和展示方式。如今我们的责任是公开审视这些历史，深化研究，进一步阐明具体作品的意义，并加强与作品来源地同行及社群的关系。博物馆不应掩盖复杂性，而应帮助人们理解它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：如今人们确实在努力正视这些物件的历史，并在适当情况下将其归还。对于这些问题以及更多相关议题，我的看法是，我们无法让时间倒流，必须找到前进的办法。接下来该怎么做？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我们都需要想出富有创意的解决方案。本月我们宣布达成一项三方协议：一位长期支持大都会非洲艺术项目的美国慈善家，将三件历史杰作的法律所有权转让给尼日利亚国家博物馆与纪念物委员会；该委员会再将作品借给大都会，至少 25 年，以便它们能在纽约得到研究和欣赏。这些作品现正陈列在 Rockefeller 展翼。今年秋天，我们也期待有机会再次迎来该委员会总干事 Olugbile Holloway。他去年参加了展翼开幕仪式，一直是我们这项合作中坚定的伙伴。", "links": [{"text": "three-way agreement", "url": "https://www.metmuseum.org/press-releases/ncmm-landmark-agreement"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "物件在流转，人也在迁徙，共同塑造了我们今天生活的世界。自 19 世纪末这些物件被交易或从原属地移走以来，离散迁徙从根本上改变了世界。我们的社群高度国际化，由来自各地的人组成；我们的机构也体现了这一点。艺术品的流传历程中可能包含许多历史悲剧，我们不该回避这些故事。我们无法扭转既成事实，但可以帮助人们理解发生过什么。根据我的经验，我们有机会呈现其文化的社群，对参与其中感到无比自豪。讲述这些故事应当提高我们对既有不公的敏感度，让我们更有同理心，并坚定不再造成新的伤害。博物馆可以是人们单纯来看美丽事物的地方，也应当让人们了解传统教育课堂上可能接触不到的人类历史面向。它们是一扇窗口，让我们看到彼此在过去和现在如何相互连结。", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Asmat 艺术家的身体面具，20 世纪中叶。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：再谈谈著名的贝宁青铜器。Andrea Emelife 是尼日利亚新建的西非艺术博物馆策展人。许多贝宁青铜器于 1897 年在所谓的“惩罚性远征”中被英国军队掠走。该博物馆希望让许多作品回到尼日利亚，并为它们及其他艺术品建造了博物馆。国际博物馆开始归还部分作品时，贝宁国王奥巴出面主张这些作品的所有权。考虑到他的家族对这些物件拥有祖传所有权，事情就更难厘清了。贝宁的这段故事产生了什么影响？接下来会怎样？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝宁艺术是世界伟大的艺术传统之一。它与欧洲文艺复兴时期的作品同时创作，创作者掌握的技术与 Donatello、Brunelleschi、Ghiberti 和 Cellini 同样精湛。贝宁艺术讲述了其他撒哈拉以南非洲传统难以讲述的故事：由于作品以耐久的铸造金属和雕刻象牙制成，我们得以看到这一传统可追溯至 14 世纪的作品范例；非洲大陆其他许多地区并没有这样的留存。对于 Alain Locke 和 W.E.B. Du Bois 等非裔美国文化史学家而言，认识到贝宁艺术的存在，对于理解自身身份及书写非洲文化遗产都至关重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们收藏了非常重要的贝宁艺术品。20 世纪 1950 年代末至 1960 年代，Nelson Rockefeller 想要建立一批杰作收藏。他在艺术市场上从经销商处及拍卖会上购入这些作品；如今它们已成为大都会非洲艺术收藏的标志。这些作品历经数代流转。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：是的，不过我记得大都会归还过几件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：2021 年，大都会主动将两件贝宁作品归还尼日利亚，并协助一位外部收藏家归还第三件作品；合作研究认定，大都会并未（或无法）取得有效所有权。这项工作促成大都会与尼日利亚国家博物馆与纪念物委员会的伙伴关系迅速发展。此后双方签署谅解备忘录，建立持续合作，其中包括一项长期计划：由尼日利亚团队参与，为该委员会的藏品进行数字化和编目。我前面提到的新借展协议，也在这一基础上迈出了意义深远的一步。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：Calder 的经销商 Klaus Perls 曾把许多这类作品捐给大都会。它们是从哪里来的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：是的，我们收藏的贝宁宫廷作品大多由 Klaus Perls 捐赠。他是一位重要的现代艺术经销商，从德国移居纽约，个人特别热衷于收藏贝宁王国艺术。他于 1991 年将收藏捐给大都会。当时，大都会对其进行了来源研究；这一研究领域在过去几十年中持续大幅发展。博物馆还举办了展览、在国际巡展，并在线发布作品及其历史。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如今，我们的新展翼展出这些作品，并将它们置于对非洲大陆各地主要艺术运动及活态传统的整体梳理之中。新的展示以当代研究为基础，也融入了大都会及世界各地专家网络的交流成果，其中尤为重要的是尼日利亚专家的声音和意见。观众可在展厅中直接阅读和聆听这些内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展翼开放当天，是疫情前以来博物馆单日参观人数最多的一天。这些作品不仅能被每年逾 600 万名到馆观众看到，也能通过网站向更多人开放，最终触达全球观众。重新开放时，我们迎来了总干事 Holloway，以及许多参与展陈工作的地区伙伴和学者；那是一个庆祝文化、社群与合作的有力时刻。我们还听到许多纽约人——他们的文化遗产正是这些作品所代表的文化——表达了深切感谢，因为他们的文化在纽约得到了礼赞。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Chief-Omas_Drum-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "一面鼓。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chief Omas，鼓，20 世纪中叶。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这里存在一种结构性的不公：这些东西都在博物馆里，可如果你回到创造它们的国家，却找不到它们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：在近几年这些作品转移之前，尼日利亚拥有的贝宁艺术藏品就已位居世界前列。该国有规模庞大的国家收藏，只是由于博物馆基础设施方面的问题，这些藏品一直未能展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们与尼日利亚合作的很大一部分，是支持其能力建设。五年前，我们曾与尼日利亚同行坦诚交流，询问他们认为我们最能在哪些方面提供帮助。他们说自己没有数字藏品数据库。于是我们开始共同投资开发一个试点数据库，并着手进行摄影记录，同时建立藏品登记档案。我们的目标是让他们收藏的数万件无可比拟的重要作品，逐步纳入这个数据库。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们有责任成为真正的伙伴，通过支持博物馆专业人员培训和开展有意义的交流来提供帮助。例如，我所在的部门会接待驻访人员，也会定期与拉各斯、哈博罗内和达累斯萨拉姆等地机构的同行共同举办工作坊。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：美国博物馆与欧洲博物馆很不一样。艺术界的每种情况都各有特殊之处。例如，一些欧洲收藏是殖民势力搜集的作品构成的；美国博物馆则是由在公开市场上购买物件的收藏家建立。我想多数人不知道，欧洲第一次非洲艺术展是什么时候举办的。1920 年是非洲艺术首次在卢浮宫办展吗？当我得知这件事时，我觉得博物馆承认非洲抽象艺术和非洲艺术对当时当代艺术的影响，真是太好了。后来我才知道，那不过是一次殖民炫耀，目的是显示法国有多强大，拥有多少异国珍宝。大英博物馆也是如此。“大英帝国的太阳永不落下”，他们收集其他地方的文化象征、纪念物和珍宝，就是为了彰显自己的强大。一方面，这些行为是错误的；另一方面，若非如此，或许这些东西都无法保存下来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我认为我们常常把这些机构的性质过度简化。一方面，它们是某些历史时期的遗产，那时人们挪用、盗窃和掠夺他人财物；另一方面，它们也属于人们拓展交流网络、努力认识自身之外世界的历史时期。那是欧洲以外传统的学术好奇心和研究的开端。今天我们之所以如此了解过去，很大程度上是因为 18、19 世纪的收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们不想过度美化启蒙运动时期，但世界的确因此变得更小。这一点也体现在各种不断丰富和扩大的博物馆收藏上。博物馆是鲜活的机构，反映着社会的热情。1870 年，纽约人决定创建一所可以通过汇集藏品了解广阔世界的机构，并由此建立了今天的大都会；这令人惊叹。它体现了人们对熟悉范围之外世界的好奇，以及亲身体验的愿望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种初衷非常值得尊重，不该被轻易搁置。真正重要的是让人们意识到，世界比他们眼前所见复杂得多。在我们生活的这个时代，这一点尤其重要：我们身处多元文化社会，也生活在全球相互依存的世界中。理解多样性以及构成我们身份的众多传统，既重要又不可替代。博物馆有责任启发我们去了解并尊重那些看似陌生、相对难以接近的文化。理想情况下，它们也能成为起点，鼓励我们走出馆舍，亲自前往文化源头。", "translated": true}]

As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. article_text:
Alisa LaGamma is the Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer Curator of the Department of the Arts of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. Few people realize that it wasn’t until the ’80s that the Met exhibited these artworks, and before that, many saw them as little more than artifacts. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. On our return from Parcours du Monde , the classic African and Oceanic art fair in Paris, last month, and not long after the one-year anniversary of the $70 million rebuild of the entire wing, it felt timely to explore a few topics in the zeitgeist.

Adam: What is the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing? Can you explain the Met’s relationship to classic African, Oceanic, and Ancient American art?

Alisa: Sure—it’s a fascinating story. In 1969 New York’s Governor Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller and the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that a new wing of the museum would be built in order to accept the gift of his collection of sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania, and the Ancient Americas. The collection had until then been housed at his Museum for Primitive Art.

This development fundamentally redefined the mission of the Met, which was then, as it is today, one of America’s leading museums. The move established that suddenly artistic traditions of three-quarters of the world, previously relegated to natural history museums, were to be recognized shoulder to shoulder with the then pinnacle of art history—the Old Masters of Western European art. Overnight the Met’s identity became that of a global institution whose aspiration was to represent all cultures.

Adam: It was a pretty radical move at the time—a major shift that changed the way we in the West see art from these huge regions of the world, and had a big impact on collectors, galleries, and museums by expanding notions of what is considered fine art. But people might not realize that the Met wasn’t on board with it at first.

Alisa: That’s right—that transformation led by Rockefeller was a hard-fought one. His enthusiasm for non-Western art was not originally shared by the Metropolitan, so actually in 1954 he established his own private institution across from the Museum of Modern Art. He was being advised by the leading specialists in what were then very young branches of art history, as he sought to assemble a survey of the major traditions absent from the Met.

Alisa LaGamma and Adam Lindemann. Photos: The Met and the author

Adam: Here’s this politician from one of the wealthiest families in the U.S., as close to American royalty as we get, and he’s asking for these objects, which were considered ethnographic material from what was then the farthest reaches of the world, to be recognized as fine art. What drove this passion of his?

Alisa: In 1930, the year Nelson graduated from Dartmouth he was made a Met trustee. The son of John D. and Abby Rockefeller, his mother had instilled in him an awareness of the important role that African and Ancient American art had played in the transformation of 20th-century art. As an internationalist and a statesman, in the years that followed he embraced learning about less familiar parts of the world through their artistic traditions. This led to his conviction that “all people have art.”

Nelson’s son, Michael, shared his father’s passion for that mission and majored in anthropology at Harvard. He was deeply and personally inspired by the cultures and art of the Pacific and pursued new avenues of inquiry into artistic practice during his travels there. We have incredibly striking Asmat sculptures he researched and collected in southwest New Guinea on view in the wing. In 1961, during his second trip to research, collect, and document the works of artists in Papua New Guinea he was in a small craft at the mouth of the Betsj River that ran out of gas and was drifting into the Arafura Sea. In attempt to swim to shore he tragically drowned.

Adam: And this is all happening in the ’60s and ’70s, when so much of the world, including the U.S., was undergoing major shifts in culture and society. How did that play into these collections coming to the Met?

Alisa: Major developments at home and abroad over the course of the 1960s relating to Civil Rights and the coming of age of new nation states across Africa were such that by 1969, Rockefeller’s campaign to incorporate non-Western art within the Met finally succeeded. In addition to the significance of the timing, the process of absorbing an existing pioneering institution into the Met was a complex one.

On a logistical level it might be considered comparable to the recent announcement of Ronald Lauder’s Neue Galerie merger . The prior Rockefeller development, however, was not simply the addition of a major private institution and epic infusion of art but one that fundamentally redefined the mission of one of America’s leading museums. It was decided that the new Met Wing would be named for Michael Rockefeller’s quest to deepen his understanding of Asmat art and over the next decade, the staff, collection, archives, and library of what had been known as the Museum of Primitive Art was transferred into the footprint of what is today the MCR Wing.

Installation view of the Arts of Africa Galleries. Photo: Bruce Schwarz

Adam: And now you’ve just last year reopened the wing after a complete renovation and rethinking of it. Of course, scholarship on art from these regions has evolved dramatically over the last few decades. But why the full renovation?

Alisa: For much of the time that the wing was under construction, Nelson Rockefeller was vice president. He died before its completion in 1982. Encompassing 40,000 square feet of galleries at what was then the southernmost frontier of the Met campus, its inaugural state-of-the-art display made minimal reference to the original cultural contexts of the works featured. Its success was such that their study blossomed in the academy and the museum’s collection expanded in new directions.

This was increasingly evident in a growing contrast between the permanent collection galleries and the groundbreaking research that we directed toward temporary exhibitions organized by the Met’s curators. It was a priority for me that those special projects that advanced deeper understanding of major traditions represented in our collection and that developed meaningful partnerships with institutions and colleagues in the regions of the world from which the works originated be reflected in the permanent collection galleries. This led me to propose a capital project to renew the Rockefeller Wing over a decade ago. A priority for my curatorial team was to reenvision our section of the museum and reintroduce the permanent collection within three independent surveys of world art that were at once grounded in history and many layers of content enriched by engagement with experts in source countries.

This is reflected in an infusion of digital content we developed to afford greater context that includes a series of three audio guides highlighting the perspectives of an international cohort of leading public intellectuals in the arts and humanities based in centers ranging from Bamako to Bogota. We also hired filmmaker Sosena Solomon to document interviews and landmarks at a dozen sites across sub-Saharan Africa featured in a series of critically acclaimed short documentaries that widen the lens on major cultural centers relevant to deeper engagement with the decontextualized works on display. That project has created all kinds of new bridges between the Met and regional partners some of which have led to signing of new memoranda of understanding, and we have followed up with a series of workshops held at museums from Gaborone to Zanzibar in which we screen the films with regional audiences.

Another important dimension of this reset is that we have leveraged the adjacencies of neighboring sections of the museum to be more meaningful. For example, the interface of the Africa galleries and those devoted to European Renaissance sculpture and decorative arts highlights works created along the coast of West Africa from the 15th century for the earliest European traders. Completed at the end of May 2025, the reinvigorated MCR Wing has shifted from its original design as a museum within a museum to a major crossroads of the museum that is at once physically and intellectually illuminated and in dialogue with adjacent galleries of Greek and Roman, European sculpture and decorative arts, and modern and contemporary art.

A horse head by a Yoruba artist from the 12th century–15th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: Met

Adam: Alisa, how long have you worked at the Metropolitan Museum?

Alisa: I have been at the museum since I was a graduate student some 31 years ago. For the last 12 of those I’ve overseen the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing and its team of specialists that I recruited to care for the three areas of the world covered by its collections. Prior to that I was simply a senior African art specialist.

Adam: You were born in Africa. Tell me how that shaped your interest in studying African art?

Alisa: My father was an American diplomat who spent his career in both Africa and Europe. He had a deep love for the many places he worked in across sub-Saharan Africa and I was born in Lubumbashi in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and spent formative years in Zambia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Togo. My family was living in Senegal, Nigeria, and South Africa when I was in college and graduate school, the period I was myself increasingly turning my focus to art history and African art.

Adam: We recently attended the annual African and Oceanic Art Fair in Paris called Parcours du Monde (“Trip Around the World”) along with a group of friends of the Met. While there we saw all the dealers and went to both the Louvre’s Cinq Continents wing and the Quai Branly Museum for world art. I thought the most interesting and provocative part of the trip was when we went to Brussels to the Royal Museum for Central Africa at Tervuren. I’ve been enjoying African art since my late 20s, and I’ve read about Belgium’s violent colonial history in King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild. Still, only then did it strike me that we’re in 2026, and they’re still sitting on thousands of objects, things taken or stolen by King Leopold II’s privateers when it was the “Congo Free State.”

Alisa: Tervuren is a unique vestige of the European colonial presence in Africa and one of its darkest chapters. It is an institution that was essentially created as a showcase for the wealth and rich natural resources of the vast territory of Central Africa to which King Leopold of the Belgians had laid claim.

Adam: In what year was this?

Alisa: This was in the late 1800s, 1898 following the temporary colonial exhibition featured at the 1897 Brussels International Exposition. It was a branch of Leopold’s propaganda. It’s not, and was never conceived of, as an art museum. It was really an institution that showcased the minerals, the woods, the wildlife, the sheer wealth of its resources. The artifacts at Tervuren reflect decades and decades of Belgian presence in that region. Many of them were things that Belgians brought back with them, after their tours of duty and then either sold to Tervuren or transferred as gifts. There were all kinds of people coming back from the Congo. You had missionaries as well as individuals who had been part of military campaigns. Some were just pure administrators, so it’s an assemblage of artifacts that reflect the Belgian presence there over an extended period of time and the result of different interactions between Belgians and residents of this region of Central Africa. Many were very violent and brutal, some of them were more benign, but it’s an especially traumatic past. Joseph Conrad was witness to the early years of the Congo Free State and he channeled his observations in the powerful critique of European colonialism that is Heart of Darkness .

Ùhúnmwèlaò (commemorative portrait) by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 16th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met

Adam: We were looking at that amazing Kongo power figure with all those ribbons on it and that gripping face. It’s an incredible masterpiece, with a story. The military privateer Alexandre Delcommune attacked chief Ne Kuko over tariffs owed when goods were coming through their regions. The dispute was about the amount charged for passage. The people’s magical fetish was confiscated. Ne Kuko wanted it back. Delcommune refused to give it back, and eventually it ends up at Tervuren. He had seized their idol, but why did he give it to Tervuren? Why didn’t he just keep it?

Alisa: He was an unregulated tradesman taking the law into his own hands in response to tariffs that were going to be introduced and levied against him. He was outraged by that and he wanted to throw his weight around. Having spent time in the region, understanding the efficacy of that object and that it had a very important psychological role in the arbitration and adjudication of cases, his seizure of it was the ultimate way of diminishing the authority of local officials. I can’t imagine that somebody like that cared about holding on to the work. It was the removal that counted as far as he was concerned.

One of the ironies of an institution like Tervuren is that we have these stories, very detailed histories of the role specific works performed in their original communities. We know a lot about the identity of this sculpture before it was removed and that in and of itself is an incredibly important piece of historical documentation. This work which is such an incredible tour de force visually is also the materialization of a conflict. The Tervuren collection can teach us so many lessons as a result of this. These are very, very precious records that shouldn’t sit in obscurity. It really should be material that is more widely accessible, and that gives us a deeper understanding of what unfolded historically.

Adam: And that raises the obvious question: What happens now? What should museums do with these collections?

Alisa: That is precisely where provenance research and sustained dialogue with colleagues and communities connected to these works become so important. At the Met, that research has long been embedded in our curatorial practice, with specialist expertise in the field developed over more than 25 years. There isn’t necessarily a single answer that applies to every object or every collection. Belgium has passed legislation concerning existing state collections and is in active discussions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo around cultural heritage and restitution that raise larger questions about access, conservation, scholarship and where works can be most meaningfully encountered. What is essential is that these histories are researched and made transparent, and that the institutions and communities most closely connected to the material are part of determining what comes next.

Iyọ́bà (queen mother) figure by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 18th century, on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met

Adam: Simply saying “send everything back” doesn’t capture the complexity nor the realities. You’re talking about an enormous country, different communities, different histories and thousands of individual objects.

Alisa: Those questions need to be worked through collaboratively rather than answered abstractly. In doing so we should not lose sight of the importance of the works themselves as cultural achievements to be respected and honored as cultural achievements.

And in a way, that brings us back to what we were talking about with the Rockefeller Wing. Museums inherited ways of collecting, categorizing and presenting works that were products of particular moments in history. Our responsibility now is to examine those histories openly, to deepen the scholarship, to deepen the presentation of the significance of specific works, and to strengthen relationships with colleagues and communities in the places where these works originated. The museum shouldn’t obscure complexity. It should help people understand it.

Adam: There’s a real effort now to reckon with the histories of these objects and, where appropriate, to return them. My view on all these things and more is that we can’t wind back the clock—we have to find a way forward. Where do we go from here?

Alisa: We all need to come up with imaginative solutions moving forward. This month we announced a three-way agreement in which an American philanthropist who has been a longtime supporter of African art at the Met is transferring her legal title to three historical masterpieces created in what is today Nigeria to its National Commission of Museums and Monuments, which is in turn loaning the works to the Met for at least 25 years so they may be studied and experienced here in New York City. These are now on view in the Rockefeller Wing, and this fall we’re looking forward to hopefully welcoming back the director general of the NCMM, Olugbile Holloway, who joined us for the opening of the wing last year and has been a steadfast partner in this work together.

Objects have circulated, and people have circulated to define the world that we live in today. Since the end of the 19th century when these objects were traded or removed from their places of origin, the world has fundamentally changed by diasporas. Our communities are highly cosmopolitan and comprised of people from all over. And so, our institutions also reflect that. There are many historically tragic events that may be a part of the path of works of art. We shouldn’t shy away from those stories. We’re not going to reverse what happened, but we can help people understand what unfolded. In my experience, communities we have had the opportunity to represent are enormously proud of their participation. Telling those stories should heighten our sensitivity to wrongs that were done and should equip us to be more compassionate and committed to not perpetuating further damage. Museums can be places where you just go to look at beautiful things, but they should also be places where you learn about dimensions of human history that you might not be exposed to in the classroom as part of your traditional education. They’re a portal to other dimensions of how interconnected we all are, both in the past and in the present.

Body mask by Asmat artist(s), mid-20th century. Photo: The Met

Adam: How about the famous Benin bronzes. Andrea Emelife is the curator of the new Museum of West African Art in Nigeria. Many of the Benin bronzes were taken by the British army in 1897 in what is called the “Punitive Expedition.” The museum sought to get many of them back to Nigeria and built a museum for them as well as other Art. When international museums started sending back certain works, the Oba (king) of Benin appeared and sought ownership of the works. Given his family’s ancestral ownership of the objects, it becomes even more complicated to unwind the situation. What’s the fallout of that Benin story and what happens now?

Alisa: Benin art is one of the world’s great art traditions. Those works were produced in parallel to works that were created in Europe during the Renaissance. They were created by artists who had a mastery of the same technology as Donatello, Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, and Cellini. They tell a story that you cannot tell with other traditions from sub-Saharan Africa because, given that they were composed of durable materials of cast metal and carved ivory, we have exemplars of creations from this tradition going back to the 14th century, which is not the case for much of the rest of the sub-continent. For African American cultural historians like Alain Locke and W.E.B. Du Bois, an awakening to the existence of Benin art was critical to their understanding of what defined their identity, and to their writing about an African heritage.

We have very important holdings of that material because, during the late 1950s through 1960s, Nelson Rockefeller wanted to put together a collection of masterpieces. He bought the works that are now icons of the Met’s African art collection on the art market—from art dealers and at auctions. These were works that had circulated over the past generations.

Adam: Yes, but the Met gave back a few, I recall.

Alisa: In 2021, the Met voluntarily returned two Benin works from the collection to Nigeria and helped facilitate the return of a third work from an outside collector, after our collaborative research determined that the Met did not (or could not) have proper title. And that effort led to a real blossoming of partnership between the Met and Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. We have since entered into an ongoing collaboration outlined in a memorandum of understanding that now includes the long-term project to facilitate the digitization and cataloguing of the NCMM’s collections together with a Nigerian team. And the new loan agreement I mentioned earlier builds on this foundation in a really powerful way.

Adam: Klaus Perls, Calder’s dealer, gave a lot of these works to the Met. Where did he get them from?

Alisa: Yes, the majority of the works in our collection from the Court of Benin were given by Klaus Perls. He was a major dealer of modern art who had immigrated to New York from Germany and his private passion was collecting art from the Kingdom of Benin. He gave his collection to the Metropolitan in 1991. At that time, the Metropolitan did provenance research, which is an area of research that has continued to advance significantly over the past few decades; exhibited the collection; toured it internationally; and published the works and their histories online.

The works in our collection are now displayed in our new wing, contextualized within our survey of major artistic movements and living traditions from across the subcontinent. The new presentation is grounded in contemporary research and exchanges with a network of experts at the Met and around the world, including, importantly, the voices and input of experts from Nigeria, which can all be read and heard by visitors right in the galleries alongside these works.

The day we opened the wing was the museum’s highest single-day attendance since before the pandemic. And the works are widely available not just to our more than six million yearly visitors, but also to an even larger number of people on our website and ultimately, they’re accessible to a global audience. When we reopened, we welcomed General Director Holloway and many partners and scholars from across the regions who we worked with on the display, and it was an incredibly powerful moment to celebrate culture, community, and collaboration. And we’ve also heard from many, many New Yorkers whose heritage this is who deeply appreciated seeing their culture celebrated here in New York City.

Chief Omas, Drum, mid-20th century. Photo: The Met

Adam: There’s a built-in injustice because all these things are in museums, but if you go back to the country that actually created them, you can’t find them.

Alisa: Nigeria has had among the largest holdings of Benin art even before all this transfer of works in the last couple of years. It has enormous national collections. They have not been visible because of issues with the museum’s infrastructure.

A huge part of our work together with Nigeria has been around supporting their capacity needs. Five years ago, we had a heart to heart with our counterparts in Nigeria and we asked them what is it that they felt we could be most helpful with. They responded that they didn’t have a digital collection database. So, we’ve been investing in creating a pilot for one with them and beginning the process of photographic documentation accompanied with accession records—the goal will be for the tens of thousands of works of incomparable importance in their collection to become part of that database over time.

We have the responsibility to help by being true partners, supporting the training of museum professionals and engaging in meaningful exchanges. For example, we host residencies in my department and periodically co-organize workshops with colleagues in institutions from Lagos to Gaborone and Dar es Salaam.

Adam: American museums are very different from European museums. Every situation in the art world is kind of a unique situation. For example, some of these European collections were built with works collected by the colonizing forces—unlike U.S. museums, which were built by collectors buying objects on the open market. I don’t think most people are aware when the first African show in Europe happened. Was 1920 the first time that African art had a show in the Louvre? When I learned this, I thought it was wonderful that the museum was acknowledging the influence of African abstraction and African art in the contemporary art of that time. I later found out this was just a colonial flex. This was to show how powerful France was, and that they possess all these exotic trophies. That’s the same with the British Museum. The sun never sets on the British Empire, and so for them to collect these cultural talismans, and monuments, and treasures from other places just showed how powerful they were. On the one hand, those actions are wrong, but on the other hand, perhaps if not for them, none of these things would have been preserved.

Alisa: I think we tend to oversimplify the nature of those institutions. On the one hand they are a legacy of periods in history when things were being appropriated, stolen, and looted. They’re also a part of the period in history when people are engaged in expanded networks of exchanges and trying to understand the world outside themselves. It’s the start of intellectual curiosity and scholarship concerning traditions outside of Europe, and we know so much today about what came before because of what was collected in the 18th and 19th centuries.

We don’t want to over glorify the Enlightenment period, but it is a fact that the world became a smaller place as a result. This is true with all kinds of museum collections that are diversifying and expanding. Museums are living institutions that reflect the passions of their societies. It’s incredible that in 1870 people in New York City decided to create an institution where they could learn about the world at large by assembling what is today the Metropolitan. It’s a reflection of people’s curiosity about the world outside of what they’re immediately familiar with, and their desire to experience it.

This is a very honorable intention that we shouldn’t just put to the side. It really is about sensitizing people to a more complicated world than the one that they’re immediately aware of. That’s an important thing, especially in the moment that we are living in, where we are a multicultural society in a globally interdependent world. It’s important and invaluable for us to understand diversity and the many traditions that define us. Museums have a responsibility to inspire us to learn about and respect cultures that appear to be foreign and relatively inaccessible to us. Ideally they are a springboard to venture beyond their walls and go to the source ourselves.

article_text:
Photographein Collective SAMPOは10月31日、11月29日、1月24日の全3回、写真を「撮る」ことだけでなく「見る」ことをめぐるワークショップを開催する。参加者持ち寄りの写真1枚を上映し、言葉にしたり、写真集を一冊のまとまりとして読む。また、作品を前にほかの人や作家と言葉を交わす ―― 写真の知識や経験にかかわらず、見ること、言葉にすること、そしてもう一度見ることを通して、写真の見え方がどのように変わるのかを参加者と一緒に体験していく。

第1回では作家・文筆家の大竹昭子が津々浦々で開催しているワークショップが予定されている。そこでは、 参加者それぞれ持ち寄った一枚の写真を上映しじっくりと見て言葉にしていく。第2回では、 現代写真集コレクターでもある鈴木雄二をゲストに迎え、和室で写真集を読み解く。そして第3回は、 参加作家による写真作品を展示し、作品を囲んで対話する。ゲストビューワーに詩人のカニエ・ナハを迎えて写真への対話を重ねていく。

本ワークショップは各回先着順での参加受付となっているため、それぞれ発売日をチェックして臨みたい。さまざまな角度から写真を「見る」ことを体感し、写真への思考を巡らせていきたい。

タイトル

article_text:
Pocket Review

Tanya Merrill's Animal Instinct

After a move upstate and a newborn, Merrill’s new work responds to the world around her.

Hyperallergic )

Two life-changing experiences lie at the heart of the captivating new oil-and-graphite paintings in Tanya Merrill’s exhibition, Land animal, house animal: The artist gave birth to her daughter in June, and her family recently relocated from New York City to upstate New York.

In her new environment, Merrill decisively challenges a pervasive anthropocentric worldview that deems humans superior and animals lesser. She foregrounds local animals as sentient beings with their own motivations and desires, including a cat in two terrific paintings, a wide-eyed and inquisitive dairy cow, and the Northern harrier (or marsh hawk) with piercing eyes and luscious gray, white, and black feathers that she frequently observes from her studio (“Marsh hawk,” 2026). This bird painting echoes regional folk art and Audubon.

article_text:
Love Actually has become one of the most quotable and memeable films of all time, but for star Keira Knightley , it’s a distant and vague memory.

In a new interview, Knightley opened up about fans approaching her and quoting the film, but it doesn’t mean much to her.

“I have not watched Love Actually since the premiere, which was when I was 18,” Knightley said in an interview with Heart . “So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody.”

She continued, “I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting Love Actually, but I don’t really know what it is. It means nothing to me.”

Knightley played Juliet, a married woman who learns her husband’s best friend, Mark (Andrew Lincoln), has feelings for her. Mark professes his love for her with giant cards, while her husband is in the next room. Juliet gives Mark a quick kiss and returns to her husband at home.

The scene is one of the most remembered, but for Knightley, it was only a week of filming when she was 17 and didn’t leave a lasting impact. In fact, in a 2024 interview with the Los Angeles Times , Knightley said one of the only lasting impressions she had of the scene was that it was “creepy” and “slightly stalkerish.”

article_text:
Source: Sara De Santis

Uta Schwietzer (third from left, holding mic), Jacqueline Sato (fourth from left) and Shen Kemin (second from right) at Mostra de São Paulo’s Audiovisual Ideas Market

A Chinese producer has said that the elevated profile of Brazilian cinema in her country has created an ideal climate for co-productions with the South American giant.

“For a long time, Chinese audiences only knew films like Central Station [1998] and City Of God [2002],” said Shen Kemin, who founded Cute Cam Pictures and serves as a representative of Shanghai Film Distribution and Exhibition Association. “But now, we’ve broadened our perspective on Brazil with The Secret Agent [2025] and I’m Still Here [2024], which were well-received.”

Shen has called for more year-round reciprocal distribution of each country’s films. “We need to expand the sale of films between our markets, going beyond the negotiations that, in practice, take place almost exclusively during international film festivals,” she said.

Jacqueline Sato, a partner and producer at the distributor Sato Company, which primarily brings Asian films to Brazil, wants to serve as a bridge between the two countries. “We have already brought in many Chinese titles, such as John Woo’s early films,” she said, “but they have always been fewer in number compared to the titles we’ve distributed from Japan and South Korea.”

Sato joined Shen and Uta Schwietzer, vice-president of Brazil’s Federation Of Audiovisual Industry And Trade (FICA) and a founding member and representative on Latin America–China Business Federation (FENLAC), on the panel ’New Markets: Co-Production And Circulation Between Brazil And China’. The session took place at the sixth Audiovisual Ideas Market, the business arm of the 50th São Paulo International Film Festival, known as Mostra de São Paulo.

Mutual cooperation

The session focused on cooperation between the countries, and looked at what is required to formalise co-productions, and what strategies Brazilian producers can adopt to secure Chinese partners after the Brazilian senate approved a film co-production agreement in July. Brazil rarely engages with China in co-productions, although panelists noted the latter’s size and ability to go head-to-head with, and at times surpass, the US in terms of audience size and box office revenue.

“It takes not only a good story, but an idea that also fits what the Chinese are looking to see in cinema today,’’ Schwietzer said. “The fact that Brazil possesses such exuberant nature also makes a big difference. There are many documentaries from Brazil that would be of interest to Chinese producers.”

July’s bilateral agreement means that films produced in partnership by production companies from both countries are considered domestic works in the Brazilian and Chinese markets, granting them access to the incentives and other benefits.

“For a co-production, there is a condition: the investment from each side must be between 20% and 80%,” Shen said. “If the Chinese company contributes at least 20% of the total budget, the Chinese government will provide benefits for the film’s production.”

Sato highlighted two films that she distributed in Brazil: The Wandering Earth (2019), which grossed approximately $700m worldwide, and prequel The Wandering Earth 2 (2023), which grossed more than $615m worldwide.

Brazilian actress Daniela Tassy played an astronaut in The Wandering Earth 2 . The casting of Tassy in the story about nations cooperating to save humanity from the threat of a rapidly-expanding Sun serves as an example of the kind of stories that can be showcased in Brazil-China co-productions.

One co-production currently underway is the animated series Ho-Ho And The Sound Of Brazil , involving CCTV Animation from China Media Group (CMG), and the Brazilian companies Amorim Filmes and LC Barreto. The series, about a Chinese panda with a passion for music who arrives in Brazil in search of new sounds, is in the final stages of production.

Brazilian João Amorim, the general director of the series, came up with the idea to co-produce with China. “For a long time I’ve wanted to enter the Chinese market, given the scale of their animation sector,” Amorim said. “Last year alone, Ne Zha 2 grossed over $2.2bn globally [with approximately 97% of the box office coming from China], a better performance than any Pixar film.”

China has been a focus at the Audiovisual Ideas Market given that 2026 marks the official China-Brazil Year of Culture.

article_text:
COWBOY BEBOP 天国の扉

劇場公開日： 2026年10月30日

解説・あらすじ

宇宙を駆け巡る賞金稼ぎたちの活躍を描いた名作テレビアニメ「カウボーイビバップ」の劇場版。ハロウィンを前にした火星の都市アルバシティーの高速道路で爆発事故が発生。それは正体不明の生物兵器を使用したバイオテロで、火星政府は首謀者に巨額の懸賞金をかけると発表する。別件でハッカーの青年を追っていたフェイは偶然にも事件現場に遭遇し、テロリストと思われる男を目撃していた。ビバップ号のクルーたちは、フェイが撮影した映像を手がかりにテロリストの正体を突き止めようとするが……。監督の渡辺信一郎や脚本の信本敬子、音楽の菅野よう子、声優の山寺宏一、林原めぐみらテレビ版のスタッフ＆キャストが再結集。

2001年製作／114分／G／日本 配給：バンダイナムコフィルムワークス 劇場公開日：2026年10月30日

その他の公開日：2001年9月1日（日本初公開）

title_original: Save Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of cars | Letters
editorial_title_zh: 拯救哈默史密斯桥——但应让其保持无车状态 | 读者来信
editorial_excerpt_zh: 读者对西蒙·詹金斯关于伦敦西部过河通道文章的回应。西蒙·詹金斯是我国历史遗产的坚定捍卫者，曾就此主题撰写过多部著作，并经常在《卫报》发文反对激进的现代建筑恶象。令人震惊的是，……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "西蒙·詹金斯是我国历史遗产的坚定捍卫者，曾就此主题撰写过多部著作，并经常在《卫报》发文反对激进的现代建筑恶象。然而，看到他竟主张拆除并重建哈默史密斯桥，仅仅是为了在道路上容纳更多的汽车（《哈默史密斯桥是我们功能失调时代的象征。资金是有的，统筹规划却不到位》，10月23日），这实在令人震惊。他声称拥堵的主要原因是“伦敦的路政施工成灾”，而实际上，这是因为有太多的汽车试图挤上一条根本不为它们设计的道路网络。", "links": [{"text": "Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/23/hammersmith-bridge-crumbling-traffic-delays-roadworks-london"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，他表示，该桥目前的状态“仅允许行人和骑行者通行”——然而每天却有12,000至15,000人使用它。重新向机动车开放该桥（越来越重的汽车对该桥目前的退化状态负有巨大责任）几乎带不来什么好处。哈默史密斯和富勒姆超过半数的家庭根本没有汽车，该地区的公共交通连接非常便利；甚至由巴恩斯-哈默史密斯电车轻运集团（Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group）提出了一项深思熟虑的计划，旨在运行无人驾驶的电动“舱式”车辆，为那些无法步行穿过哈默史密斯桥的人提供服务。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "且不说拆除一座二星级*保护建筑（Grade II* listed structure）所涉及的巨大困难（我们那位勇敢的历史遗产捍卫者现在在哪儿呢？），在为了容纳更多汽车而付出巨额成本去重建它时，根本没有一个切实可行的商业论据。无论是出于环保还是健康原因（特别是考虑到它们造成的污染），整体的重点都应该放在减少对汽车的依赖上。要是权力机构中能有人鼓起勇气来对付汽车游说集团就好了。理查德·卡特（Dr Richard Carter）博士，英国伦敦普特尼", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "西蒙·詹金斯严厉批评了各个未能在一时期内（7年时间）重建哈默史密斯桥的伦敦当局，这是正确的。欧洲没有第二个首都允许主要交通干线长期中断、阻止车辆过河。伦敦并非单一管理区（unitary authority），其市长也没有其他首都同行那样筹集资金来支付新桥费用的权力。缺乏统筹规划似乎已经深深根植于各个相关当局的规划流程中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伦敦西南部这种令人遗憾的状况，导致了上里士满路（Upper Richmond Road）沿线长期的交通混乱，以及上下班高峰期普特尼高街（Putney High Street）如炼狱般的拥堵。要不是英国人对所谓的“遗产”项目有着迷恋，我们多年前就能拥有一座能够承载交通的临时桥梁了。相反，为了对维多利亚时期工程壮举的错置怀旧，市民们被迫走过或骑过一座摇摇晃晃的桥才能到达对岸。朱利安·海迪（Julian Heddy），英国伦敦东申", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "西蒙·詹金斯（Simon Jenkins）关于哈默史密斯桥那篇偏颇的文章配发了一张过时的照片，给人以年久失修之感，而现实却大不相同。得益于哈默史密斯和富勒姆区议会投资的£55m，这座标志性的二级*级列入保护建筑已找到了作为慢行交通通道的成功新用途，每天有15,000人步行和骑行穿过其重新开放的主车道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据我所知，并没有什么“日益增长的舆论”呼吁将其拆除重建。恰恰相反，当地稳定的倾向已经转变为在此成功基础上再接再厉，提出引入一支轻型、自动驾驶的电动穿梭巴士车队，以填补公共交通空白，确保所有居民都能舒适安全地过河。社区主导的巴恩斯-哈默史密斯电车轻运（Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit）正与欧米奥英国（Ohmio UK）及合作伙伴合作来实现这一愿景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与该桥对机动车关闭之前相比，邻近桥梁及更广泛道路网上的交通量有所下降，而在电动自行车革命的助推下，巴恩斯（Barnes）的当地经济正在蓬勃发展。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "花费数亿资金恢复污染严重、危险且具排他性的过境交通，是没有任何可信的商业理由的。随着市长将到2030年减少27%的汽车交通量定为目标，当务之急是巩固这一成功，而不是将其毁掉。查尔斯·坎皮恩（Charles Campion），巴恩斯-哈默史密斯电车轻运主席", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4e6adc0446ddc28be7edfab522c8959e76ff6775/0_0_3500_2334/master/3500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "千禧桥，于2001年开通。", "caption": "千禧桥，于2001年开通。摄影：多米尼克·利平斯基/PA", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "西蒙·詹金斯是一位备受尊敬的伦敦历史遗产与建筑环境评论员，对维护历史基础设施的成本有着深刻理解。我们认同他对伦敦桥梁的承诺，但不认同他关于如何使用伦敦桥梁基金会（City Bridge Foundation）慈善资金的观点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们维护着横跨数个世纪工程历史的五座泰晤士河桥梁：伦敦塔桥、伦敦桥、萨瑟克桥、千禧桥和黑衣修士桥。它们的维护需要持续的投资和承诺，我们目前对黑衣修士桥耗资£15m的翻修工程便是一个证明，其中包括修复2,000多个铸铁栏杆并重新粉刷整个结构。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们的捐赠基金旨在永久履行这些职责。它既不是伦敦基础设施的一般性基金，其价值也不是衡量可自由支配资金多少的标准。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在维护和支持我们的桥梁之余，若有可用资金，我们还会向致力于解决伦敦各地不平等和弱势问题的慈善机构提供资助。这些资金用于慈善目的，并受适用于我们工作的法律和监管安排管辖。它们不能被简单地重新分配，去支付超出我们职责范围的桥梁的修复或重建费用。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们认识到伦敦的桥梁对每天依赖它们的民众的重要性，但其他泰晤士河过江通道属于其他组织的责任。我们通过行业组织与负有责任的机构分享知识和经验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "近900年来，“桥梁之屋产业”（Bridge House Estates）的传统一直在帮助维持伦敦桥梁的耸立，同时支持整个城市的慈善工作。我们为这一传统以及与我们并肩致力于建设一个更公正的伦敦的慈善伙伴感到自豪。保罗·马蒂内利（Paul Martinelli），城市桥梁基金会主席", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "交通政策", "links": [{"text": "Transport policy", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/politics/transport"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "交通", "links": [{"text": "Transport", "url": article_text:
Simon Jenkins is a great defender of our national heritage, having produced many books on the subject and frequently written in the Guardian against aggressive modern architectural horrors. How shocking, then, to find him arguing for the replacement of Hammersmith Bridge simply to provide for yet more cars on the roads ( Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October ). He claims that the principal cause of congestion is “London’s epidemic of roadworks”, when actually it’s the fact that there are just too many cars trying to use a road network that isn’t designed for them.

Furthermore, he says that, in its present state, the bridge “merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross it” – and yet between 12,000 and 15,000 people use it every day. Reopening it to motor traffic (and increasingly heavy cars have massively contributed to the current state of degradation of the bridge) would bring little benefit. Well over half the households in Hammersmith and Fulham don’t have access to a car, and there are very good public transport links in the area; there is even a well-thought-out plan put forward by the Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group to run driverless electric “pod” vehicles to provide for those who are unable to walk across Hammersmith Bridge.

And quite apart from the huge difficulty involved in enabling the tearing down of a Grade II* listed structure (where’s our doughty defender of national heritage now?), there is no effective business case for replacing it at enormous cost to provide for yet more cars, when for both environmental and health reasons (particularly because of the pollution they cause), the whole emphasis should be on reducing our reliance on cars. If only someone in authority would summon up the courage to tackle the motoring lobby. Dr Richard Carter Putney, London

Simon Jenkins is right to castigate the different London authorities that have failed to replace Hammersmith Bridge over a period of seven years. No other capital city in Europe would allow such a prolonged truncation of a major transport artery, preventing vehicles from crossing the river. London is not a unitary authority and its mayor does not have the powers of his peers in other capitals to raise the finance to pay for the cost of a new bridge. The lack of joined-up thinking appears to be baked in to the planning processes of the different relevant authorities.

This sorry state of affairs in south-west London has led to permanent traffic chaos along the Upper Richmond Road and the hell that is Putney High Street during rush hour. Were it not for the British obsession for so-called “heritage” projects, we could have had a temporary bridge capable of carrying traffic years ago. Instead citizens are obliged to walk or pedal their way across a wonky bridge in order to get to the other side for the sake of a misplaced nostalgia for Victorian engineering feats. Julian Heddy East Sheen, London

The outdated photograph published with Simon Jenkins’s off-beam article on Hammersmith Bridge suggests decrepitude, when the reality is quite different. Thanks to £55m of investment by Hammersmith and Fulham council, this iconic, Grade II* listed bridge has found a successful new purpose as an active travel crossing, with 15,000 people a day walking and wheeling across its reopened main carriageway.

I know of no “growing body of opinion” calling for its replacement. On the contrary, the settled local preference has moved to build on this success with a proposal to introduce a fleet of lightweight, autonomous electric shuttles to fill the public transport gap to ensure all residents can cross comfortably and safely. Community-led Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit is working with Ohmio UK and partners to deliver this vision.

Traffic on neighbouring bridges and the wider road network is down compared with before the bridge closed to motor vehicles, while Barnes’s local economy is booming, aided by the ebike revolution.

There is no credible business case for spending hundreds of millions bringing back polluting, dangerous and exclusionary through traffic. With the mayor targeting a 27% reduction in car traffic by 2030, the priority must be to build on this success, not undo it. Charles Campion Chair, Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit

Simon Jenkins is a respected commentator on London’s heritage and built environment, with a deep understanding of the costs of maintaining historic infrastructure. We share his commitment to London’s bridges, but not his views on how the City Bridge Foundation’s charitable funds should be used.

We maintain five Thames bridges: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium and Blackfriars, spanning centuries of engineering history. Their upkeep requires sustained investment and commitment, demonstrated by our current £15m Blackfriars Bridge refurbishment, repairing more than 2,000 cast-iron balusters and repainting the entire structure.

Our endowment exists to meet these responsibilities in perpetuity. It is not a general fund for London’s infrastructure, nor is its value a measure of money freely available to spend.

Alongside maintaining and supporting our bridges, where there are funds available, we make grants to charities tackling inequality and disadvantage across London. These funds are made for charitable purposes and governed by the legal and regulatory arrangements that apply to our work. They cannot simply be redirected to pay for the restoration or replacement of a bridge outside our remit.

We recognise the importance of London’s bridges to the people who rely on them every day, but other Thames crossings are the responsibility of other organisations. We share knowledge and experience with those responsible through industry groups.

For nearly 900 years, the legacy of Bridge House Estates has helped keep London’s bridges standing while supporting charitable work across the city. We are proud of this legacy and the charity partners working alongside us to build a fairer London. Paul Martinelli Chairman, City Bridge Foundation

article_text:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. MUBI opens “ Fatherland ” in select theaters starting Friday, October 23.]

After two Telluride Film Festival tributes, Sandra Hüller left the mountains to return to her hometown of Leipzig, Germany, where she is raising a 15-year-old daughter and directing a play. She’s still adjusting to her global rising star status. She’s directing because she has given up on theater acting.

The comedy “Toni Erdmann” put her on the map in 2016, followed by her Oscar-nominated role as a woman accused of killing her husband in Justine Triet’s “Anatomy of a Fall” (2023). She also earned raves as a bovine Nazi wife in “The Zone of Interest” that year.

In 2026, she took on four movies, two black-and-white European projects and two big-budget Hollywood blockbusters. She won the Berlinale Silver Bear for her performance as a 17th-century war veteran living as a man in Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose ” (MUBI), followed by her first studio gig as Eva Stratt, the scientist assigned to save the world in blockbuster “Project Hail Mary” (Amazon/MGM). And she returned to Cannes in Pawel Pawlikowski’ s “Fatherland” (MUBI) as Erika Mann, the car-driver daughter of Nobel Prize-winning novelist Thomas Mann.

“Fatherland” offers a mere slice of the scion Erika Mann, wealthy, privileged, educated, who could warrant a film of her own. The fact that she was married to the gay British poet W.H. Auden is a throwaway in the film, in which she serves as her elderly father’s assistant and representative on a 1949 post-war road trip back to East and West Germany. She’s in charge.

“She’s a race car driver, amongst other things,” said Hüller over coffee. “She’s also an author, journalist, an actor. Pawel wanted her to be a part of this journey because, in reality, she wasn’t. It was somebody else in the car. He wanted her to be the person responsible.”

The Buick was a monster. “It’s really heavy,” said Hüller. “It takes some effort to drive it. Because we don’t have help with the steering wheel. It takes some muscle.” That’s what sets the German actress apart from the field. She’s tall, lithe, intelligent, androgynous, vulnerable, and powerful all at once.

“Fatherland” kicks off with a bravura five-and-a-half minute locked-off single take of Klaus (August Diehl) in Cannes, sitting naked on the floor by a bed with a sleeping young man. He talks on the phone with Erika, who tries to coax her depressed drug-addict intellectual twin to come on a road trip with her back to Germany as his father accepts the Goethe prize. Hüller had long wanted to work with Diehl but had to settle for a phone call from her kitchen. (They will work together on another German film, about the painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and his partner Erna Schilling.)

Central to the journey is the dynamic between the father and the daughter, because she’s really angry with him. “When I read their letters to each other,” said Hüller, “they were what we say schonungslos . They didn’t spare each other from criticism. They were open, but they were forgiving each other at the same time. It was a deep, respectful love that they had, and a beautiful relationship. They are in a big conflict with each other at that point of their lives, and it’s painful because they love each other so much. When this loved person is dying, and they don’t agree on how to deal with it, that is devastating.”

According to Hüller, many German films have tried to portray the Manns, “but it’s a complicated family structure,” she said, “and also a complicated moral question around them. They left Germany during the war because it was too dangerous, and as we can see in the film, some people still didn’t forgive them. So it’s a discussion: What would you do if you were privileged? Would you use this privilege, or would you say, ‘I don’t care, I’ll stay here and watch everybody die.’ It’s a big topic.”

Erika Mann’s own homosexual relationships are only slightly referenced. “The person that she meets, this other journalist,” said Hüller, “she’s been in a relationship with her before, and they broke up for I can’t remember the reason. That’s also part of her freedom: not to talk about who she is and what she prefers, and I admire that.”

In one party scene in a night club Mann has a memorable face-off with her ex-husband Gustaf Gründgens, an actor who stayed behind and collaborated with the Nazis. “We always try to imagine ourselves as these superior creatures that do everything right,” said Hüller, “but we actually don’t know what we would do in a situation like this. Joachim Meyerhoff who was playing Gründgens, is an idol for me in German theater. He’s somebody whom we all know, and it was a great choice to let him play this person. I felt honored that I was allowed to slap him in the face, if you know what I mean.”

“Rose” is a less expressive role. No temper tantrums allowed. Blending into a strict rural community required discipline and rigor. When does this woman disguised as a man pee? How does she satisfy her wife? (She acquired dildos during her decade as a soldier in the 30 Years War.) As constrained as the character is, the actress shows us what she is feeling. “This is kind of a defect,” said Hüller. “I can’t hide what I feel. Like never, which is sometimes difficult in life. Even if I wanted to. But in this case, I felt like her whole existence after she chose to live in men’s clothes and to have the identity of a man to the outside, I don’t even know what her inner identity is. She has to be so aware of everything around her that she’s more a spectator of everything than an active subject.”

Survival was key. “She has to have a 360 degrees view of everything all the time,” said Hüller, “because she should never come into a situation where she has to act in a rush or where she would use gestures that are not appropriate for her chosen character. So it had to be contained. She’s coming from a long war. There’s a lot of damage and grief and darkness inside that person. And what I love about her the most is that she’s able to transform it into something soft, in a way. I loved her for not becoming this harsh, hard, cynical person.”

Next up the actress is taking on the portrayal of a man, German artist Wolfgang Herrndorf, in Maria Schrader’s “Work And Structure.” “It’s different because he’s not hiding anything,” said Hüller. “He’s just Wolfgang Herrndorf. I’m playing a man, but not trying to play a man. I look androgynous. I was born this way, and sometimes I can profit from it, not always, but sometimes.”

For her first studio gig, she took on powerful project director Eva Stratt in “ Project Hail Mary ,” assigned to save the world. After Hüller met Phil Lord and Chris Miller in London, she felt she could work with them. “I had no idea how to play her,” she said. “I was thinking about somebody completely different who could inhabit this strength and responsibility and clarity. But there are moments when other people think you can do it. You start to think you can do it yourself. But I would never have thought that somebody would think of me in a character like that.”

While she had to make some adjustments to working on a big-budget Hollywood movie, “I was surprised that there was so much freedom,” she said. “I would have expected it to be much more formal and more delivery oriented, but it wasn’t. And it had a lot to do with the people who were working on this because Chris and Phil are playful and open directors, and they give a lot of space to explore things. And Ryan [Gosling] is somebody who loves that too. So I never felt pressed into something that I don’t belong in. I was lucky.”

While the new idea of Stratt singing karaoke at a party threw her at first, Hüller came around. It happened because Gosling heard her singing on set. She loves to sing. “It’s annoying for people around me,” she said. “My daughter is always rolling her eyes. At first I thought, ‘why would she? it’s not her thing. It’s not her position to do that.’ But then I thought, ‘yeah, maybe that’s interesting that she’s leaving that position for that particular moment.'”

Hüller searched the libraries of goodbye songs. And producer Amy Pascal suggested a few songs that she was sure she could clear. “The next night, I found [Harry Styles’ song “Sign of the Times”] and sent it to her and asked if she could she could make this possible and she did. And the next day we shot it.”

The upcoming “Digger” (Legendary/Warner Bros.) is another big studio project, where Hüller plays the half-sister of Tom Cruise for one of her favorite directors, A.G. Iñárritu. “He’s very energetic,” she said. “He’s leading this whole shooting day in a way that you want to keep up with him. It’s inspiring to see him and his energy and his commitment to what he’s doing, and he’s sharing thoughts about everything. He’s trying things. Sometimes we do things completely different on another day. So he’s looking for the best thing that can happen.”

She enjoyed working with the “focused” Cruise, but did not hang out with him. “I felt like these two chose each other, the director and the actor. They really wanted to do this together. That was great to watch.”

The actress made the transition to directing at her Leipzig theater group last year. “I’m part of a theater collective of people who have known each other also for 20, 30 years,” she said. “Because the reception of my appearance on stage has changed a little bit through this public eye, I didn’t feel safe on stage anymore. The decision to go to the other side was a good decision because there’s so much to learn, and I enjoy it. I might go back. But I took some time to adjust my expectations. I went to the theater to be part of a group, but when you’re in this exhibited position, I didn’t know how to deal with that, and maybe I’ll be ready in the coming years to own that different position that I have. But I was a bit heartbroken that I lost it.”

One aspect of stardom that Hüller has embraced is red carpet fashion. “I have a team with Jordan Johnson Chung, who is choosing the outfits for me,” she said. “And I’m lucky to work with Chanel and people who help me with hair and makeup. But for me, in my life, I like to get up and get out of the house without anything. It’s always a bit of an adjustment to make. But when we do it, it’s fun.”

The promo tour for “Digger” will pull her back in. And the award season beckons. “It’s a challenge to find the balance between your personal life and decisions,” she said. “I don’t have a team around me when I’m at home. I have things to do. But I also want to help the films wherever I can. So I have to try and find the balance between. All of these things come with responsibility. It’s hard for me to to step away from that, like when a studio says, ‘But it’s your responsibility to be at that press day.’ No, it’s not.”

The actress is picky about her projects and has turned many things down, she said: “Not enough, some people think. I roll my eyes when I have to bring emotional value to a project that doesn’t genuinely have it. So if a script isn’t good, but I’m asked to make it good with acting, that’s something that I’m not here for. I don’t like that.”

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Seventeen-year-old DOC NYC , America’s largest documentary festival, has revealed its influential 15- film Short List. The festival will run its main lineup of 118 features, 26 world premieres, 27 U.S. premieres, and 89 short films in-person November 11 – 19 in New York City’s IFC Center, SVA Theatre, and Village East by Angelika and continues online through November 29 with films available to viewers across the U.S. All the films will have theatrical screenings at the festival, often with the directors in person.", "links": [{"text": "DOC NYC", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/doc-nyc/"}, {"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Historically, most of the DOC NYC shortlist titles overlap with the Academy’s official 15-film Oscar shortlist. With the notable exception of Netflix’s Oscar-winning “My Octopus Teacher,” for 14 of the last 15 years, the festival has screened the documentary that went on to win the Academy Award, including “Mr Nobody Against Putin,” “No Other Land,” “20 Days in Mariupol,” “Navalny,” “Summer of Soul,” “American Factory,” “Free Solo,” “Icarus,” “O.J.: Made in America,” “Amy,” “Citizenfour,” “20 Feet from Stardom,” “Searching for Sugar Man,” and “Undefeated.”", "links": [{"text": "DOC NYC shortlist", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/festivals/doc-nyc-awards-short-list-the-eternal-memory-little-richard-i-am-everything-1234917771/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B2706.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Arash Ashtiani, Pegah Ahangarani and Brent Lang at IndieWire Art of the Doc 2026 held at Lumen on October 19, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/202605733_1_RWD_1920.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Who Killed Alex Odeh?", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And the festival has screened 64 of the last 75 Oscar-nominated documentary features. DOC NYC’s Short List: Features selection committee is overseen by Artistic Director Jaie Laplante and Director of Special Projects Thom Powers. Last year, DOC NYC had over 100 submissions for the short list. In the end four of the five Documentary Feature Oscar nominees came from the list, and overall 11 of the shortlisted titles came from the list. The year before was their best, as they predicted 14 out of 15."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We haven’t hit 15 out of 15 yet,” said Laplante on Zoom. “But we got really close. This is the ring that we’re chasing every year. We’re aware that this is one of the first lists to start to define the doc race. The power of the list is that it suggests the 15 films that the doc branch absolutely needs to watch before they decide to vote.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While the Short Lists sections showcase a selection of nonfiction features and shorts that the festival’s programming team considers to be among the year’s strongest contenders for Oscars and other prizes, the Winner’s Circle is a celebration of films already awarded at major international film events that they deem worthy of additional consideration. Selects Encore showcases significant titles from DOC NYC’s year-round Selects screening series.", "links": [{"text": "Oscars", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/oscars/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DOC NYC’s 2025 Short List screenings will include two New York City premieres: Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazic’s “To Hold a Mountain,” winner of the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize: Documentary at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and recently chosen to represent Montenegro in the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards , and Mehrdad Oskouei and Soraya Akhlaghi’s “A Fox Under a Pink Moon,” executive produced by David Borenstein (co-director of the Oscar-winning DOC NYC 2025 alumnus “Mr Nobody Against Putin”).", "links": [{"text": "Awards", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/awards/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Winner’s Circle screenings include the NYC premiere of Pegah Ahangarani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” winner of the L’Œeil d’Or for Best Documentary at Cannes and recently selected as the UK submission for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Movies that overlap both the ten Critics Choice Association (CCA) Feature Documentary nominees and DOC NY Short List of 15 are particularly strong future awards contenders. The CCA nominees for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards were announced Tuesday and include DOC NYC-listed “14th” (NYFF, Netflix), David Greaves’ archival “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” (Sundance, Neon), Alex Gibney’s four-hour biodoc “ Musk ” (Venice, Bleecker/HBO), the self-distributed Israeli exposé “Naza” (Venice), and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “ You Can See Everything ” (Telluride, A24).", "links": [{"text": "Critics Choice Association (CCA) Feature Documentary nominees", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/results/critics-choice-documentary-awards-2026-nominations-14th-1235221592/"}, {"text": "Critics Choice Documentary Awards were announced Tuesday", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/results/2025-critics-choice-documentary-awards-nominations-orwell-1235155687/"}, {"text": "", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/orwell-2-2-5-review-raoul-peck-documentary-1235122470/"}, {"text": "Musk", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/musk/"}, {"text": "You Can See Everything", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/you-can-see-everything/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ava DuVernay’s “14th” is a follow-up of sorts to Oscar-nominated documentary “13th,” laying out the ways the United States government is currently flouting the post-Civil War Constitutional amendment. “It’s certainly as powerful and as hard-hitting and of the moment,” said Laplante. “Ava is a force in nature now, in terms of her personality. I’m expecting this will get a lot of attention.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Laplante was impressed with the “incredible research” that went into “Musk,” he said, “incredibly comprehensive. A lot of that, of course, we know from the news. But when you see it all together, and you see the way that Alex Gibney lays it out, it takes on a force of its own, and it’s an undeniable film.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The programmer saw “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” at Sundance. “I didn’t want to leave that party,” he said. “It felt so fresh and so contemporary, like it was happening in front of you. That’s a really strong contender.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s controversial “You Can See Everything,” “It’s absolutely a wild film,” said Laplante. “Lance has a cinematic eye. He tethers the movie into cinema. The fusion of Nathan’s absurdist artistic viewpoints creates something new and cinematic. It’s an exciting collaboration between these two artists. A lot of new doc branch members are excited by this type of new energy that they’re bringing to this film. Reenactments are not an uncommon thing in documentary.
