article_text:
Seventeen-year-old DOC NYC , America’s largest documentary festival, has revealed its influential 15- film Short List. The festival will run its main lineup of 118 features, 26 world premieres, 27 U.S. premieres, and 89 short films in-person November 11 – 19 in New York City’s IFC Center, SVA Theatre, and Village East by Angelika and continues online through November 29 with films available to viewers across the U.S. All the films will have theatrical screenings at the festival, often with the directors in person.

Historically, most of the DOC NYC shortlist titles overlap with the Academy’s official 15-film Oscar shortlist. With the notable exception of Netflix’s Oscar-winning “My Octopus Teacher,” for 14 of the last 15 years, the festival has screened the documentary that went on to win the Academy Award, including “Mr Nobody Against Putin,” “No Other Land,” “20 Days in Mariupol,” “Navalny,” “Summer of Soul,” “American Factory,” “Free Solo,” “Icarus,” “O.J.: Made in America,” “Amy,” “Citizenfour,” “20 Feet from Stardom,” “Searching for Sugar Man,” and “Undefeated.”

And the festival has screened 64 of the last 75 Oscar-nominated documentary features. DOC NYC’s Short List: Features selection committee is overseen by Artistic Director Jaie Laplante and Director of Special Projects Thom Powers. Last year, DOC NYC had over 100 submissions for the short list. In the end four of the five Documentary Feature Oscar nominees came from the list, and overall 11 of the shortlisted titles came from the list. The year before was their best, as they predicted 14 out of 15.

“We haven’t hit 15 out of 15 yet,” said Laplante on Zoom. “But we got really close. This is the ring that we’re chasing every year. We’re aware that this is one of the first lists to start to define the doc race. The power of the list is that it suggests the 15 films that the doc branch absolutely needs to watch before they decide to vote.”

While the Short Lists sections showcase a selection of nonfiction features and shorts that the festival’s programming team considers to be among the year’s strongest contenders for Oscars and other prizes, the Winner’s Circle is a celebration of films already awarded at major international film events that they deem worthy of additional consideration. Selects Encore showcases significant titles from DOC NYC’s year-round Selects screening series.

DOC NYC’s 2025 Short List screenings will include two New York City premieres: Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazic’s “To Hold a Mountain,” winner of the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize: Documentary at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and recently chosen to represent Montenegro in the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards , and Mehrdad Oskouei and Soraya Akhlaghi’s “A Fox Under a Pink Moon,” executive produced by David Borenstein (co-director of the Oscar-winning DOC NYC 2025 alumnus “Mr Nobody Against Putin”).

The Winner’s Circle screenings include the NYC premiere of Pegah Ahangarani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” winner of the L’Œeil d’Or for Best Documentary at Cannes and recently selected as the UK submission for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards.

Movies that overlap both the ten Critics Choice Association (CCA) Feature Documentary nominees and DOC NY Short List of 15 are particularly strong future awards contenders. The CCA nominees for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards were announced Tuesday and include DOC NYC-listed “14th” (NYFF, Netflix), David Greaves’ archival “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” (Sundance, Neon), Alex Gibney’s four-hour biodoc “ Musk ” (Venice, Bleecker/HBO), the self-distributed Israeli exposé “Naza” (Venice), and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “ You Can See Everything ” (Telluride, A24).

Ava DuVernay’s “14th” is a follow-up of sorts to Oscar-nominated documentary “13th,” laying out the ways the United States government is currently flouting the post-Civil War Constitutional amendment. “It’s certainly as powerful and as hard-hitting and of the moment,” said Laplante. “Ava is a force in nature now, in terms of her personality. I’m expecting this will get a lot of attention.”

Laplante was impressed with the “incredible research” that went into “Musk,” he said, “incredibly comprehensive. A lot of that, of course, we know from the news. But when you see it all together, and you see the way that Alex Gibney lays it out, it takes on a force of its own, and it’s an undeniable film.”

The programmer saw “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” at Sundance. “I didn’t want to leave that party,” he said. “It felt so fresh and so contemporary, like it was happening in front of you. That’s a really strong contender.”

As for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s controversial “You Can See Everything,” “It’s absolutely a wild film,” said Laplante. “Lance has a cinematic eye. He tethers the movie into cinema. The fusion of Nathan’s absurdist artistic viewpoints creates something new and cinematic. It’s an exciting collaboration between these two artists. A lot of new doc branch members are excited by this type of new energy that they’re bringing to this film. Reenactments are not an uncommon thing in documentary. It’s perfectly legit.”

This year’s selections for Short List: Features are:

“14th” (Netflix) Director: Ava DuVernay Producers: Ava DuVernay, Spencer Averick, Tammy Garnes, Paul Garnes A powerful film essay exploring the legacy of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

“American Doctor” (Watermelon) Director: Poh Si Teng Producers: Poh Si Teng, Kirstine Barfod, Reem Haddad A visceral, unflinching film following three notable U.S. physicians as they provide in-person support at a Gaza hospital treating victims of mass-casualty events from the Israeli war campaign.

“The Bend in the River” (Netflix) Director: Robb Moss Producers: Lisa Remington, Kristin Feeley A masterful meditation on the eternal, the temporal and the inevitable, from veteran filmmaker Robb Moss.

“Everybody to Kenmure Street” (Icarus) Director: Felipe Bustos Sierra Producer: Ciara Barry An uplifting portrayal of resistance focuses on an incident in 2021 when immigration officers conducted a raid on Glasgow’s Kenmure Street.

“A Fox Under a Pink Moon” (NYC Premiere) Directors: Mehrdad Oskouei, Soraya Akhlaghi Producer: Mehrdad Oskouei A young, talented Afghan woman living under the thumb of the patriarchy in Iran channels her emotions into unforgettable expressions of art.

“The Great Experiment” (DOC NYC Selects) Directors: Stephen Maing, Eric Daniel Metzgar Producers: Stephen Maing, Eric Daniel Metzgar, Farihah Zaman Traversing the U.S. from 2016 to 2020, patient observational filmmaking becomes a temperature check on American democracy—what George Washington described as the last great experiment in promoting human happiness in civil society. Co-director Stephen Maing will receive the Robert and Anne Drew Award for Documentary Excellence at this year’s DOC NYC Visionaries Tribute.

“Musk” (Bleecker, HBO Documentary Films) Director: Alex Gibney Producers: Alex Gibney, Jessie Deeter, Erin Edeiken, Zhang Xin, Joey Marra, Nick Shumaker, Jessica Grimshaw, Dana O’Keefe An epic work profiling the world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk. Director Alex Gibney will receive the Lifetime Achievement Award at this year’s DOC NYC Visionaries Tribute.

“Naza” Directors: Yuval Abraham, Rachel Szor Producers: Harry Davies, Lindsay Poulton, James Wilson Anonymous members of the Israel Defense Force candidly reflect on their attitudes toward civilian casualties, known as NAZA, and how they process the meaning of genocide.

“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” (Neon) Director: David Greaves Producers: Liani Greaves, Anne de Mare A glorious night, capturing a vital period of American culture, when luminaries who had been active in the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s recount their memories.

“One in a Million” (Frontline/PBS) Directors: Itab Azzam, Jack MacInnes Producers: Will Anderson, James Bluemel, Andrew Palmer, Raney Aronson-Rath A chronicle of one Syrian daughter’s journey in fleeing war and seeking refuge in Germany, and how over ten years, new pressures and opportunities present themselves.

“Soul Patrol” (Kino Lorber) Director: J.M. Harper Producers: Sam Bisbee, Danielle Massie, J.M. Harper, Nasir Jones, Peter Bittenbender A hidden chapter of American military history—the Vietnam War’s first Black special ops team, an elite unit operating deep behind enemy lines.

“Time and Water” (NatGeo) Director: Sara Dosa Producers: Shane Boris, Elijah Stevens, Jameka Autry, Sara Dosa\ A letter to the next generation by an Icelandic poet, reflecting on the melting glaciers that are a harbinger of climate change.

“To Hold a Mountain” (NYC Premiere, Sales Title) Directors: Biljana Tutorov, Petar Glomazić Producers: Biljana Tutorov, Petar Glomazić, Quentin Laurent, Rok Biček In the remote highlands of Montenegro, the spirit of motherhood, the violence of men, and the sacredness of the mountain collide and reconcile.

“Wild Inside” (Sandbox, HBO Documentary Films) Director: Penny Lane Producers: Gabriel Sedgwick, Nickolas Hasse In 2023, Flaco the Eurasian Eagle Owl became an international folk hero and a mythological figure for a world in which so many find themselves living in circumstances far away from their roots.

“You Can See Everything” (A24) Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Producers: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose, Jack Davis As she prepares to begin serving her federal prison sentence, disgraced Silicon Valley tycoon Elizabeth Holmes continues to claim she has never lied, as America’s premiere absurdist documentarians record her every word.

SHORT LIST: SHORTS The Short List: Shorts showcase of 15 titles is now in its ninth year at DOC NYC. The selection process is overseen by Artistic Director Jaie Laplante, Director of Special Projects Thom Powers, and consultant Samah Ali. In 2025, the showcase included “All The Empty Rooms,” which went on to win the Oscar.

This year’s selections for Short List: Shorts are:

“The Baddest Speechwriter of All” Directors: Ben Proudfoot, Stephen Curry Producers: Stephen Curry, Erick Peyton, Ben Proudfoot At 93, Martin Luther King Jr. ‘s lawyer and speechwriter offers a living testament to history, and reminds us that silence is still our most urgent problem.

“The Boys and the Bees” Director: Arielle Knight Producer: Sean Weiner On an idyllic farm in rural Georgia, beekeeping parents tenderly share their knowledge of life, love, and nature with their young sons while restoring their homestead.

“Buckskin” Director/Producer: Mars Verrone A ground-breaking African American and indigenous forester reflects on his life’s work of conservation and ancestral knowledge, while he approaches the twilight of his days.

“A Derailment” Director: Nathan Truesdell Producers: Kat Nguyen, Will Lennon A 2023 freight train derailment in rural Ohio gives rise to a shocking new low in corporate malfeasance.

“The Grandfather Puzzle” Director: Ora DeKornfeld Producers: Zsofia Paczolay, Noémi Veronika Szakonyi, Máté Artur Vincze Ora wants to better understand her aging grandfather before it’s too late. When she travels to Hungary to see if she can unlock the mysteries of his defense mechanisms, she finds a world left behind that illuminates a deep appreciation for life as it is now.

“La Tierra Del Valor (The Home of the Brave)” Director: Cristina Costantini Producers: Cristina Costantini, Alfie Koetter In the face of growing antipathy toward immigrants, Latina pop star NEZZA makes the bold choice to perform the National Anthem at Dodger Stadium in Spanish, sparking an outpouring of outrage, support, and discussion about freedom of speech and who decides what ‘American’ means.

“Listen” Director: Taliesin Black-Brown Producers: Taliesin Black-Brown, Sam Davis, Greg Moga An Alaskan sound specialist works for preservation within two levels of loss – the fading songs of wildlife disappearing from the wilderness, as climate change threatens natural populations; and his mother’s disappearing memory, as she slowly succumbs to dementia.

“The Oath” Directors: Liane Aviram, Louis Hollis Producer: Liane Aviram Dr Lina Qasem-Hassan, a Palestinian living and working in Israel, teaches medical ethics as well as practicing as a physician – walking a tightrope of activism and professionalism while working through the trauma of her people.

“One Last Order” Directors: Lauren Defilippo, Sam Soko Producers: Lauren Defilippo, Sam Soko, Amanda Pollak After 37 years at Mac’s Drive-Thru in Gainesville, Florida, sunny and beloved Sighle is retiring. As customers travel from near and far to say goodbye, this heartwarming portrait celebrates an everyday worker who always went above and beyond, and the joy and community one person can inspire.

“An Open Field” Director: Teboho Edkins Producers: Don Edkins, Carine Chichkowsky One hundred and fifty seven people died when a new Boeing 737 MAX crashed in Ethiopia in 2019. While Boeing callously deflects blame for their negligence, a family of one victim finds strength in gathering collective mourning.

“Outposts – Nothing Here Is Yours” Director: Hilla Medalia Producers: Hilla Medalia, Sheila Nevins, Yael Melamed In the West Bank, Palestinian shepherd communities face escalating settler violence and displacement, while a group of Israeli activists stand in solidarity with shepherd communities as they struggle to remain on their land.

“The Revolution Against Death” Director: Joshua Oppenheimer Producer: Signe Byrge Sørensen A sharp, provocative look at the anti-aging industry and our increasingly elaborate efforts to resist mortality.

“They’re Here” Directors: Laura Poitras, Rachel Lauren Mueller Producers: Rachel Lauren Mueller, Laura Poitras, Yoni Golijov A view of the evils of ICE through an organized resistance group of citizens in Minneapolis during the 2025-26 winter, using a unique cinematic language.

“The Tuners” Director: Pawel Piotr Chorzepa Producer: Joanna Chorzepa Behind the scenes of Warsaw’s Chopin Festival, a group of expert tuners vie to achieve the perfect pitch so that the champion pianist will win on their instrument.

“Water Cooler” Director/Producer: Emma V.F. In the halls of NYC’s immigration court, the casual chitchat of ICE agents waiting to arrest their unsuspecting targets stands in stark contrast to the horrors these detainees are likely to face.

WINNER’S CIRCLE The DOC NYC Winner’s Circle for documentary features, introduced in 2019, highlights films that arrive at DOC NYC with significant awards pedigrees already in place. Past films shown in Winner’s Circle that all went on to further acclaim include “Writing with Fire,” “The Mole Agent,” “A House Made of Splinters,” “Hollywoodgate,” “In the Rearview,” “Bad Axe,” “Midnight Family,” and “Advocate.” To qualify for inclusion in this category, films must have won a major award at a significant international or US film festival.

This year’s selections for Winner’s Circle are: “American Pachuco: the Legend of Luis Valdez” Director: David Alvarado Producers: David Alvarado, Lauren DeFilippo, Everett Katigbak, Amanda Pollak Against political resistance and industry skepticism, Luis Valdez pushes Chicano storytelling forward, creating iconic works that challenge, celebrate, and expand America’s story. Winner, Audience Award: U.S. Documentary and Festival Favorite Award, 2026 Sundance Film Festival

“Bucks Harbor” Director: Pete Muller Producers: Pete Muller, Nathan Golon, Noel Paul Striking cinematography marks this observant, verite film about men in East Maine, the traditions of their elders, and their complex inner lives. Winner, Golden Eye Award for Best Documentary Film, 2026 Zurich Film Festival

“Closure” Director: Michał Marczak Producers: Monika Braid, Remi Grellety, Michał Marczak, Katarzyna Szczerba, Karolina Marczak A haunting portrait of what it means to seek closure that’s a testament to parental love. Winner, Golden Alexander International Competition Award, 2026 Thessaloniki International Documentary Festival

“An Eye for an Eye” Directors: Tanaz Eshaghian, Farzad Jafari Producers: Christoph Jorg, Katayoon Arsanjani, Gelareh Kiazand, Joey Marra A tense examination of Iran’s justice system and one family torn asunder by a legacy of abuse and mariticide, unfolding like a Shakespearean tragedy. Winner, Grand Prize Impact Documentary, 2026 Fipadoc

“Give Me the Ball!” Directors: Liz Garbus, Elizabeth Wolff Producers: Liz Garbus, Elizabeth Wolff, Chris James, Dan Cogan, Dominic Crossley-Holland, Gentry Kirby Billie Jean King, the iconic athlete who changed both the worlds of tennis and of women’s athletics, offers new perspectives on her legacy and the state of the sports world. Winner, Audience Award / Best Documentary Feature, 2026 Provincetown International Film Festival

“Nuisance Bear” Directors: Gabriela Osio Vanden, Jack Weisman Producers: Will N. Miller, Michael Code, Teddy Leifer, Jack Weisman, Gabriela Osio Vanden\ The modern clash between human beings and polar bears takes on an ironic meaning when an Inuit elder shares his perspectives on the ancient belief and customs of his people. Winner, U.S. Documentary: Grand Jury Prize, 2026 Sundance Film Festival

“Rehearsals for a Revolution (NYC Premiere)” Director: Pegah Ahangarani Producers: Parnian Farnam, Pegah Ahangarani, Arash Ashtiani Celebrated Iranian actor Pegah Ahangarani creates an essayistic documentary, weaving together home movies and news broadcasts to construct a vivid portrait of Iran’s modern history in the four decades since the revolution. Winner, L’Œil d’or Documentary Award, 2026 Cannes Film Festival

“Steal This Story, Please!” Directors: Carl Deal, Tia Lessin Producers: Carl Deal, Tia Lessin, Karen Ranucci, Diana Cohn, Caren Spruch Amy Goodman of Democracy Now! pursues the news with integrity and dauntlessness, seeing independent journalism as a major force for good. Winner, Greg Gund Memorial Standing Up Competition, Cleveland International Film Festival

SELECTS ENCORE Selects Encore showcases a selection of films that screened at DOC NYC Selects, the festival’s ongoing screening series extension that runs annually from late winter through summer. The films chosen for Selects Encore represent works that continue to be present in the season’s awards conversations.

This year’s selections for Selects Encore are:

“Daylight” Director: Jon Kasbe Producers: Jon Kasbe, Zoe Rogovin Serving a life sentence for murder, Joe Garcia finds unexpected refuge in Taylor Swift’s lyrics. When an essay he writes about love and music goes viral, it cracks open the past and rekindles a connection, opening the door to a life and love he thought were lost forever.

“A Life Illuminated” Director: Tasha Van Zandt Producers: Tasha Van Zandt, Sebastian Zeck, Jessica Harrop, Kathryn Everett A daring quest to document a bioluminescent phenomenon that could forever change how we understand life on Earth. “Manhood” Director: Daniel Lombroso Producers: Kerry Mack, Rebecca Shaid Manhood explores shame, sex, and the fragile myths of American masculinity, with dark humor and unexpected empathy.

“Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World” Director/Producer: Sasha Waters If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it, and Sasha Waters’ beguiling portrait is as poetic as its protagonist.

“Scenes From the Divide” Director: Alison Klayman Producers: Alison Klayman, Courtney Powell A fierce battle among American Jews over identity, history, and responsibility is revealed in the homes of New Yorkers on both sides of Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral campaign.

“Theydream” Director: William D. Caballero Producers: William D. Caballero, Brad Jones, Erin Ploss-Campoamor, Elaine Del Valle A deeply personal documentary that examines the transformative nature of grief for a close-knit Puerto Rican family.

“Who Moves America” Director: Yael Bridge Producers: Yael Bridge, Jeremy Flood, Yoni Golijov, Mars Verrone\ Examines the tense 2023 contract negotiations between UPS and its 340,000 unionized workers, as a microcosm for the larger struggles of labor justice in the U.S.A.
excerpt_original: The DOC NYC Short List is often predictive of December's eventual Oscar shortlist. Films that are also nominated for Best Feature at the Critics Choice Award Documentary Awards get a leg up for future non-fiction awards.

title_original: Tokyo Docs Looks Beyond Japan as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” Seek International Paths in Busan
editorial_title_zh: Tokyo Docs 致力于将目光投向日本以外，随着《Call & Response》与《Mission100》在釜山寻求国际发展道路
editorial_excerpt_zh: Tokyo Docs 的今村健一（Kenichi Imamura）探讨了如何将日本纪录片推向全球，同时《Call & Response》与《Mission100》在釜山展示了各自的项目。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Tokyo Docs 致力于将目光投向日本以外，随着《Call & Response》与《Mission100》在釜山寻求国际发展道路", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tokyo Docs 的今村健一（Kenichi Imamura）探讨了如何将日本纪录片推向全球，同时《Call & Response》与《Mission100》在釜山展示了各自的项目。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "日本纪录片界从来不缺愿意将数年生命奉献给某个主题的电影人。然而，根据 Tokyo Docs 联合创始人今村健一（Kenichi Imamura）的说法，这里往往缺少一种能够将这些电影带出日本的结构。这不仅是 2011 年成立的国际提案平台 Tokyo Docs 越来越关注的焦点，也是较新的 J-Docs Hub 的重点所在，该机构旨在为日本纪录片创作者提供开展国际工作所需的技能、人脉和开发支持。今村目前担任 J-Docs Hub 的常务董事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Imamura-WS-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在釜山接受 Asian Movie Pulse 采访时，今村描述了一个在本土比局外人想象的要健康的日本纪录片界。他提到，在最近的一年里，有近 100 部日本纪录片获得了院线发行，但他强调，其中许多电影的制作和发行方式仍然非常自给自足。导演们经常自己筹集资金、独自拍摄和剪辑，在东京的一两家小影院上映，然后花费相当大的精力逐渐拓展到另外十家或二十家场地。这些电影确实存在，其中许多也很强劲，但它们的创作者往往几乎完全是为了日本观众而构思它们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对今村而言，这是一个 Tokyo Docs 多年来一直试图解决的错失良机。“我想推动他们走向世界，”他解释道。日本创作者支援基金（Japan Creator Support Fund）提供的支持的到来，为进一步发展这一雄心提供了机会。J-Docs Hub 作为 Tokyo Docs 旗下的多年期倡议而建立，其核心是国际开发，而不仅仅是个人的提案环节。官方项目将其三个阶段描述为学习、网络和创作（Learning, Networking and Creating），涵盖了从项目开发和筹款到海外市场以及实际制作开发支持的一切内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第一部分是教育。项目实验室（Project Lab）精选了少量项目，由制片人埃里克·尼亚里（Eric Nyari）领导开展为期一年的流程，期间电影人将学习如何构建提案文稿（pitch decks）和预告片，以及如何在国际行业活动中展示他们的项目。其他倡议则专门针对制片人，而藤冈朝子（Asako Fujioka）的纪录片目的地研讨会（Documentary Destinations seminars）则探讨了电影人在电影完成后应该做什么：哪些电影节、市场、教育平台和发行途径可能真正适合某部特定的纪录片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第二阶段是切实的国际曝光。今村提到支持团队参加印尼的 Docs by the Sea，以及前往柏林、戛纳、伊赫拉瓦（Ji.hlava）的“新兴制片人”项目（Emerging Producers program）和 IDFA 学院的电影人和制片人。其目的不仅仅是资助一次旅行，而是让日本纪录片专业人士亲身体验真正形成国际合拍、销售和电影节关系的各种环境。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第三阶段关乎开发本身。虽然这些支持不能直接用作制作资金，但它可以涵盖与开发相关的拍摄、剪辑、旅行和指导。今村特别感兴趣的是建立一个系统，使获得的知识不会停留在最初的参与者手中。获得国际经验的电影人可以作为导师回馈给下一代，从而使信息得以流通，而不是在单个资助周期结束时一再消失。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "选择哪些项目能够走出国门并不一定很简单。今村最初倾向于寻找那些表面上似乎与日本以外有相关性的主题。然而，深度本土化纪录片的成功使这一假设变得复杂。一个故事可能只涉及一个日本家庭，却依然能够与别处的观众产生强烈的共鸣。对他而言，更重要的特质越来越在于：电影人是否真心想要进入那种国际对话——去寻找外国制片人、跨越边界合作，并重新思考该项目如何触达不同的观众。英语会有所帮助，但动机更为重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在釜山展示的这两个项目恰好说明了对具有国际相关性的日本纪录片的这种定义可以多么广泛。一个深入日本社会罕见的机构内部；另一个则跟随一位痴迷的自由潜水刺鱼者跨越海洋，去追求一个几乎不可能实现的目标。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "“Call & Response”：坂上香（Kaori Sakagami）将镜头对准日本封闭的惩教系统", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Call-and-Response.jpg", "alt": "《Call & Response》剧照", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "坂上香（Kaori Sakagami）对将镜头伸入日本惩教机构的艰难早已不陌生。她早期的作品《Prison Circle》拍摄于公私合营监狱——岛根朝日社会复归促进中心，该机构是一个公私合营的监狱，并审视了一个私人部门组织参与安全和职业培训等领域的机构，而监狱本身仍属于公共惩教系统的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们在釜山交谈时，坂上香小心翼翼地将这种安排与同美国相关的私有监狱模式区分开来。日本监狱仍然是公共机构；某些业务是外包给私营公司的。她感兴趣的是，即使是这种有限的存在，能否将不同的思考引入一个极其僵化的系统。在她看来，私营部门的参与在一定程度上使某些做法不那么封闭，而更广泛的监狱官僚机构仍然对变革保持抗拒。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "坂上指出，管理囚犯待遇的规则与习俗具有惊人的持久性。虽然已经进行过法律改革，但制度惯例的存续时间往往远超立法本身。她认为，部分问题在于监狱与日本普通社会之间的隔阂。由于监禁人口相对较少，且惩教设施基本不对公众开放，监狱的状况很容易被归为关乎“他们”而非“关乎我们”的事情。社会冷漠与信息匮乏的结合，使得极端的纪律和过时的规章得以延续，而无需经受长期的公众讨论。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的新纪录片《Call & Response》将镜头转向少年感化学校，并通过说唱工作坊作为一种手段，让年轻人能够表达那些通常难以直接抒发的经历。完成后的日文版时长229分钟，分为上下两部分，延续了坂上倾向于给机构及身处其中之人充足时间、使其超越抽象概念的创作偏好。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影近四小时的时长，首先且最直接地与坂上所记录的那场实验的前所未有性密不可分。日本少年惩教设施内部的工作坊为年轻参与者创造了一种自由度，这在此类环境中曾经几乎是难以想象的。坂上并没有将这个过程压缩为一系列高光片段，而是希望细致记录这种自由是如何随时间推移而发展的：参与者如何对其做出反应、人际关系如何发生变化，以及当那些通常受到严格机构控制的年轻人被赋予更大空间来表达自我时会发生什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一点尤为重要，因为正如坂上所解释的那样，日本的惩教机构长期以来一直根据一种根深蒂固的假设在运作，即赋予年轻人更多的自由会导致他们变得无法管教。该片试图通过工作坊的具体过程来检验这一假设，而不仅仅是进行反驳。与此同时，超长的片长也让坂上得以揭示环绕在参与者周围的更广泛制度结构，包括平时鲜少接受公众审视的种种惩戒形式和根深蒂固的做法。在我们进行采访时，日本院线版将保留其大约四个小时的时长，且已有二十多家影院承诺上映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让这个项目特别契合今村所描述的更广泛使命的原因在于，这部电影从一个非常具体的日本体制出发，却触及了远超于此的问题：社会期望惩罚达成什么目的、为什么机构之外的人对被困其中的人漠不关心、以及如果没有双方之间的沟通，重返社会是否可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "《Mission100》：一口气、一支长矛、五年追逐的一场执念", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Mission-100.jpg", "alt": "Mission 100 Banner", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果说《Call & Response》探讨的是一个几乎完全封闭的环境，那么《Mission100》则走向了相反的方向：进入一个广阔无垠、变化莫测的自然空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "制片人大崎健太郎本人就是一名休闲自由潜水打鱼者，这个项目始于一次巧合。在2020年，当他在日本的一个小岛上露营时，他与自由潜水打鱼者小坂训平住在同一家民宿。未来的导演和另一位摄影师当时也在那里，出于不相关的原因。谈话最终转向了小坂非凡的雄心：通过自由潜水猎捕体型日渐庞大的鱼类，并最终尝试用单手长矛捕获一条100公斤重的犬齿金枪鱼。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大崎立刻意识到，这超出了适合做成YouTube视频的素材范畴。他本就被小坂捕获猎物的规模所震撼——虽然大崎可能会觉得一条8公斤重的鱼已经不小了，但小坂追求的是重达30、40或50公斤的动物，并且最终目标直指100公斤以上。然而，更重要的是其背后的哲学。小坂给自己设定了规矩，并以一种在纯粹性上近乎不理性的强度接近大海。这种执念成为了拍摄一部长篇纪录片的理由。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也使得小坂成了一个有时令人气恼的纪录片主角。大崎形容他是那种几乎完全忠于自己个人意愿、而在处理其他事情时却极其靠不住的人。会议可能会被忘掉、承诺可能会被打破、电话可能会被忽视。甚至连发送赞助商所需照片这样最基本的事情，都可能变成一场挣扎。大崎半开玩笑地称他为一个“社会不适应者”，但正是这种让制作变得困难的特质，也让这个人物引人入胜：他的自私与纯粹源自同一个根源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "小坂最终达成了100公斤的目标，但大崎并不认为那是这个故事的自然结局。捕获这条鱼从来都不是为了创纪录或赢得比赛。他内心更深切的渴望是遭遇那些他尚未了解的自然切面。一旦某个看似不可能的目标达成，另一个未知依然存在。他继续旅行、自由潜水，并正考虑在一个地方定居，以便将这项实践融入他作为渔夫的生活中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "结合来看，《Call & Response》和《Mission100》有力地印证了今村的坚持：日本纪录片不应被过于简单地划分为能够走向海外的题材和不能走向海外的题材。一部是关于惩罚、沟通以及围绕受监禁青少年的社会隔阂的体制电影；另一部则是关于一个将整个生命围绕着“屏住一口气潜入海洋”这一行为来组织的男人的冒险纪录片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "连接它们的并非题材，而是投入度，以及将这种投入度带入国际语境的意愿。这归根结底正是东京纪录片大会（Tokyo Docs）和 J-Docs Hub 试图改变的地方。日本电影人长期以来展现出愿意花费数年时间独自拍摄、剪辑和筹资讲述故事的准备。今村的关切在于接下来会发生什么：这些故事是留在狭小的本土发行圈内，还是终于具备了走向外部的基础设施。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Tokyo Docs Looks Beyond Japan as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” Seek International Paths in Busan"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tokyo Docs’ Kenichi Imamura discusses taking Japanese documentaries global, as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” present their projects in Busan."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Japanese documentary cinema has never lacked filmmakers willing to devote years of their lives to a subject. What it has often lacked, according to Tokyo Docs co-founder Kenichi Imamura, is a structure capable of taking those films beyond Japan. That is increasingly the focus not only of Tokyo Docs, the international pitching platform launched in 2011, but also of the newer J-Docs Hub, which is designed to give Japanese documentary filmmakers the skills, contacts and development support necessary to work internationally. Imamura currently serves as managing director of J-Docs Hub."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Imamura-WS-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse in Busan, Imamura described a Japanese documentary scene that is healthier domestically than outsiders might assume. He cited close to 100 Japanese documentaries receiving theatrical releases in a recent year, but stressed that the way many of those films are made and distributed remains remarkably self-contained. Directors frequently finance projects themselves, shoot and edit alone, open in one or two small Tokyo cinemas and then spend considerable effort expanding gradually to another ten or twenty venues. The films exist, and many are strong, but their creators often conceive them almost exclusively for Japanese audiences."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Imamura, that is the missed opportunity Tokyo Docs has spent years trying to address. “I want to push them to go to the world,” he explains. The arrival of support through the Japan Creator Support Fund offered a chance to develop that ambition much further. J-Docs Hub was established as a multi-year initiative under Tokyo Docs, with international development rather than simply individual pitching sessions at its center. The official program describes its three stages as Learning, Networking and Creating, covering everything from project development and fundraising to overseas markets and support for actual production development."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The first part is education. The Project Lab selects a small number of projects for a year-long process led by producer Eric Nyari, during which filmmakers learn how to construct pitch decks and trailers and how to present their projects at international industry events. Other initiatives concentrate specifically on producers, while Asako Fujioka’s Documentary Destinations seminars examine what filmmakers should do once a film is completed: which festivals, markets, educational platforms and distribution routes may actually suit a particular documentary."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The second stage is practical international exposure. Imamura mentioned supporting teams attending Docs by the Sea in Indonesia, as well as filmmakers and producers traveling to Berlin, Cannes, Ji.hlava’s Emerging Producers program and IDFA Academy. The purpose is not simply to finance a trip, but to allow Japanese documentary professionals to experience the environments in which international co-production, sales and festival relationships are actually formed."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The third stage concerns development itself. article_text:
Tokyo Docs Looks Beyond Japan as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” Seek International Paths in Busan

Tokyo Docs’ Kenichi Imamura discusses taking Japanese documentaries global, as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” present their projects in Busan.

Japanese documentary cinema has never lacked filmmakers willing to devote years of their lives to a subject. What it has often lacked, according to Tokyo Docs co-founder Kenichi Imamura, is a structure capable of taking those films beyond Japan. That is increasingly the focus not only of Tokyo Docs, the international pitching platform launched in 2011, but also of the newer J-Docs Hub, which is designed to give Japanese documentary filmmakers the skills, contacts and development support necessary to work internationally. Imamura currently serves as managing director of J-Docs Hub.

Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse in Busan, Imamura described a Japanese documentary scene that is healthier domestically than outsiders might assume. He cited close to 100 Japanese documentaries receiving theatrical releases in a recent year, but stressed that the way many of those films are made and distributed remains remarkably self-contained. Directors frequently finance projects themselves, shoot and edit alone, open in one or two small Tokyo cinemas and then spend considerable effort expanding gradually to another ten or twenty venues. The films exist, and many are strong, but their creators often conceive them almost exclusively for Japanese audiences.

For Imamura, that is the missed opportunity Tokyo Docs has spent years trying to address. “I want to push them to go to the world,” he explains. The arrival of support through the Japan Creator Support Fund offered a chance to develop that ambition much further. J-Docs Hub was established as a multi-year initiative under Tokyo Docs, with international development rather than simply individual pitching sessions at its center. The official program describes its three stages as Learning, Networking and Creating, covering everything from project development and fundraising to overseas markets and support for actual production development.

The first part is education. The Project Lab selects a small number of projects for a year-long process led by producer Eric Nyari, during which filmmakers learn how to construct pitch decks and trailers and how to present their projects at international industry events. Other initiatives concentrate specifically on producers, while Asako Fujioka’s Documentary Destinations seminars examine what filmmakers should do once a film is completed: which festivals, markets, educational platforms and distribution routes may actually suit a particular documentary.

The second stage is practical international exposure. Imamura mentioned supporting teams attending Docs by the Sea in Indonesia, as well as filmmakers and producers traveling to Berlin, Cannes, Ji.hlava’s Emerging Producers program and IDFA Academy. The purpose is not simply to finance a trip, but to allow Japanese documentary professionals to experience the environments in which international co-production, sales and festival relationships are actually formed.

The third stage concerns development itself. While the support cannot simply be used as production financing, it can cover development-related shooting, editing, travel and mentorship. Imamura is particularly interested in creating a system in which the knowledge gained does not remain with the original participants. Filmmakers who acquire international experience can return as tutors for the next generation, allowing information to circulate rather than repeatedly disappearing when a single funding cycle ends.

Choosing which projects can travel internationally is not necessarily straightforward. Imamura initially tended to look for subjects that obviously seemed to have relevance outside Japan. Yet the success of deeply local documentaries has complicated that assumption. A story may concern a single Japanese family and still connect powerfully with audiences elsewhere. For him, the more important quality is increasingly whether the filmmaker genuinely wants to enter that international conversation: to seek foreign producers, collaborate across borders and rethink how the project might reach different audiences. English helps, but motivation matters more.

The two projects presented in Busan illustrate exactly how broad that definition of internationally relevant Japanese documentary can become. One looks inside institutions that Japanese society rarely sees; the other follows an obsessive spearfisher across oceans in pursuit of an almost impossible goal.

“Call & Response”: Kaori Sakagami Turns the Camera Toward Japan’s Closed Correctional System

Kaori Sakagami is already familiar with the difficulty of getting a camera inside Japan’s correctional institutions. Her earlier “Prison Circle” was filmed at the Shimane Asahi Social Reintegration Center, a public-private partnership prison, and examined an institution where private-sector organizations participate in areas including security and vocational training while the prison itself remains part of the public correctional system.

During our conversation in Busan, Sakagami was careful to distinguish this arrangement from the privately owned prison model associated with the United States. Japanese prisons remain public institutions; certain operations are contracted to private companies. What interests her is whether even that limited presence can introduce different thinking into an extraordinarily rigid system. In her view, private-sector involvement has made certain practices somewhat less closed, while the broader prison bureaucracy remains resistant to change.

Sakagami points to the remarkable longevity of rules and customs governing the treatment of prisoners. Legal reform has occurred, but institutional habits can survive far longer than legislation. Part of the problem, she argues, is the distance between prisons and ordinary Japanese society. With a comparatively small incarcerated population and correctional facilities largely closed to public observation, prison conditions are easily framed as something concerning “them” rather than “us”. A combination of social apathy and lack of information allows extreme discipline and outdated protocols to continue without sustained public discussion.

Her new documentary, “Call & Response”, shifts the focus toward juvenile training schools and uses rap workshops as a means through which young people can articulate experiences that are frequently difficult to express directly. The completed Japanese version runs 229 minutes, divided into two parts, continuing Sakagami’s preference for giving institutions and the people inside them enough time to become more than abstractions.

The film’s nearly four-hour running time is first and foremost connected to the unprecedented nature of the experiment Sakagami was documenting. The workshops inside Japan’s juvenile correctional facilities created a degree of freedom for the young participants that would previously have been almost unimaginable within such an environment. Rather than compressing the process into a series of highlights, Sakagami wanted to record carefully how that freedom developed over time: how the participants responded to it, how relationships changed and what happened when young people who were normally subjected to strict institutional control were given greater space to express themselves.

This was particularly important because, as Sakagami explains, Japanese correctional institutions have long operated according to a deeply ingrained assumption that giving young people greater freedom would cause them to become uncontrollable. The film attempts to test that assumption through the concrete process of the workshops rather than simply arguing against it. At the same time, the extended running time also allows Sakagami to expose the broader institutional structures surrounding the participants, including forms of discipline and deeply established practices that rarely receive public scrutiny. The Japanese theatrical version will retain its approximately four-hour duration, with more than twenty cinemas already committed to screening it at the time of our conversation.

What makes the project particularly suited to the broader mission Imamura describes is that the film begins with a very specific Japanese system but reaches questions far beyond it: what society expects punishment to accomplish, why people outside an institution remain indifferent to those trapped within it, and whether rehabilitation is possible without communication between the two sides.

“Mission100”: One Breath, One Spear and Five Years Following an Obsession

If “Call & Response” deals with an almost completely closed environment, “Mission100” heads in the opposite direction: into an enormous, unpredictable natural space.

Producer Kentaro Osaki is himself a recreational spearfisher, and the project began through coincidence. In 2020, while camping on a Japanese island, he stayed at the same guesthouse as spearfisher Kunpei Kosaka. The future director and another photographer were also there for unrelated reasons. Conversation eventually turned toward Kosaka’s extraordinary ambition: hunting increasingly enormous fish through freediving and eventually attempting to take a 100-kilogram dogtooth tuna with a single hand spear.

Osaki immediately recognized that this was larger than material suitable for a YouTube video. He was already impressed by the scale of Kosaka’s catches—while Osaki might consider an eight-kilogram fish substantial, Kosaka was pursuing animals weighing 30, 40 or 50 kilograms and ultimately aiming beyond 100. More important, however, was the philosophy behind it. Kosaka imposed his own rules on himself and approached the sea with an intensity that seemed almost irrational in its purity. That obsession became the reason to make a feature documentary.

It also makes Kosaka an occasionally infuriating documentary protagonist. Osaki describes him as someone who is almost completely faithful to whatever he personally wants to do and remarkably unreliable when asked to deal with anything else. Meetings can be forgotten, promises broken and phone calls ignored. Even something as basic as sending a photograph required for a sponsor can become a struggle. Osaki jokingly describes him as a “social misfit”, but the same quality that makes production difficult also makes the character compelling: his selfishness and purity come from the same place.

Kosaka eventually achieved the 100-kilogram goal, but Osaki does not see that as the natural ending of the story. Catching the fish was never primarily about establishing a record or winning a competition. His deeper desire is to encounter aspects of nature he does not yet know. Once one apparently impossible target has been reached, another unknown remains. He continues traveling and spearfishing and is considering settling somewhere where he can make the practice part of his life as a fisherman.

Taken together, “Call & Response” and “Mission100” make a useful argument for Imamura’s insistence that Japanese documentaries should not be divided too easily into subjects that can travel and subjects that cannot. One is an institutional film about punishment, communication and the social distance surrounding incarcerated young people; the other is an adventure documentary about a man who organizes his entire existence around descending into the ocean on a single breath.

What connects them is not subject matter but commitment, along with a willingness to let that commitment enter an international context. This is ultimately what Tokyo Docs and J-Docs Hub are trying to change. Japanese filmmakers have long demonstrated that they are prepared to spend years shooting, editing and financing stories on their own. Imamura’s concern is what happens next: whether those stories remain inside a small domestic circuit, or whether the infrastructure finally exists for them to move outward.

article_text:
News

Man Killed by Falling Debris at Frank Lloyd Wright’s Arizona Home

Winds reportedly dislodged the piece of roofing material that struck Rogério Renato Mateucci, a Brazilian university rector.

A piece of roof material struck and killed Rogério Renato Mateucci, a Brazilian university rector, while he was on a walking tour of architect Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West in Scottsdale, Arizona, on Friday, October 16.

Heavy winds dislodged the piece of debris that struck the educator, who died instantly, a spokesperson with the Scottsdale Police Department told Hyperallergic . His death is currently under investigation as a weather-related incident, the spokesperson added.

Mateucci had been the rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná in Brazil since 2022 , and earned multiple degrees in higher education leadership as a member of the Marist Catholic order.

"The Foundation extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the individual who died," the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation, which owns and operates the property, said in a statement shared to Instagram . "No further details will be shared out of respect for privacy and to allow officials to complete their work. The property is closed to the public until further notice."
excerpt_original: Winds reportedly dislodged the piece of roofing material that struck Rogério Renato Mateucci, a Brazilian university rector.

article_text:
Issue

New Currents: Taiki Yokote

TAIKI YOKOTE ’s

Floating Rubble / Coco, Sen , 2022, rubble, mixed media, dimensions variable, at “even a worm will turn,” parcel, Tokyo, 2022. Photo by Hidehiko Omata. Courtesy the artist.

The detritus of ordinary life prevails in Taiki Yokote’s work. From plastic bags and bicycle covers to rebar and rubble, the Tokyo-based artist attends to the things we discard or overlook once they are no longer of use. He gathers these derelict items like a curious archaeologist; then, with the dexterity of an engineer, transforms them into strange, kinetic installations that examine not only the affective values we assign to materials, but also the tender memories they hold.

Floating Rubble / Coco, Sen (2022), at first glance, appears to be a sprawling, jumbled heap of debris—the kind of waste one might come across while walking past a construction site or an abandoned building. It is a deceptively unassuming configuration, until subtle movements catch the eye: concrete slabs hover mid-air, weightless, rotating gently, almost autonomously. The gravity-defying phenomenon recurs throughout Yokote’s oeuvre, achieved through built-in magnets whose like poles repel each other. In Wriggling Blue - Tower (2022), a totem-like column is shrouded in blue tarp and secured with rope, rippling nonstop as hidden mechanical components squirm beneath, trying to break free. By animating inert scraps, Yokote presents forsaken objects as entities that exist in their own right, beyond our verdicts of expiration, carrying precious histories that will quietly outlast us.

article_text:
Rachel Feldman’s “ Lilly, ” starring Patricia Clarkson , will open the third edition of the Women and the World International Film Festival , which runs in London from Nov. 5-12.

Highlights of the program, which puts women’s authorship at its center, include the world premiere of Sigrid Andrea P. Bernardo’s “Laya,” alongside premieres of Marina Kunarova’s “The Nomad’s Legacy” and Flaminia Graziadei’s “A Year in London.”

Related Stories

Emmys Move to Prime Video in Six-Year, Global Deal Worth Around $15 Million a Year

In a statement, Ksenia Bugrimova, the festival director, said, “The age of the ‘good girl’ is over. Cinema needs women who are complicated, instinctive, ambitious, vulnerable, fearless and free – women who do not ask permission to take up space.

“We believe there should simply be more films by women in the world – and more opportunities for those films to reach audiences. Celebrating women is important, but celebration alone is not enough. We want to support them, advocate for them and connect their work directly with audiences and the international film industry.”

The jury includes David Gyasi, British actor and producer; Olwen Fouéré, Irish actor, writer and director; MyAnna Buring, British-Swedish actor; Elena Andreicheva, documentary filmmaker and producer; Denise Parkinson, VP, sales and marketing global, Variety; David Martinez, film publicity executive; Rebecca del Tufo, co-founder and co-director, ScreenCraft Works; and Victoria Emslie, British actor and producer.

In addition to the screening program, WWIFF said it is expanding its efforts to provide a platform for emerging filmmakers and creative talent through collaborations with University College London, LAMDA, Film London and BFI Network.

The festival’s 2025 edition attracted 2,450 attendees and closed with the U.K. premiere of Scarlett Johansson’s directorial debut “Eleanor the Great.”

title_original: REGINA JOSÉ GALINDO: LOS PEORES TIEMPOS POSIBLES
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "A través de 33 obras realizadas desde 1999, la artista guatemalteca Regina José Galindo explora las huellas de la guerra, el genocidio, el racismo y la violencia patriarcal, utilizando su cuerpo como soporte de inscripción de la violencia y como instrumento de denuncia. La exposición, que se podrá ver hasta el 15 de noviembre en el Museo del Chopo de la Ciudad de México, conecta distintas geografías y temporalidades para mostrar cómo las estructuras de dominación siguen operando sobre los cuerpos y la memoria colectiva."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "El cuerpo ha sido, desde sus primeras acciones a finales de los años noventa, el principal medio de denuncia e intervención política de Regina José Galindo (Ciudad de Guatemala, 1974). A través de la performance, la artista confronta las estructuras de poder y las formas de violencia que impactan la experiencia individual y colectiva: la represión estatal, el racismo, el colonialismo, el patriarcado y la guerra."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Su práctica se ha desarrollado en relación estrecha con la historia reciente de Guatemala, marcada por el conflicto armado interno (1960-1996) y el genocidio contra la población maya, pero sus preocupaciones desbordan las fronteras nacionales para establecer conexiones con otras geografías y contextos violentos."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "En sus acciones, el cuerpo funge como soporte y vehículo de una memoria que no pertenece únicamente a quien la encarna. Galindo lo expone a situaciones de vulnerabilidad, sometimiento y riesgo para hacer visibles mecanismos de dominación que, con frecuencia, permanecen naturalizados o se expresan a través de discursos políticos, cifras y abstracciones. El carácter físico de sus performances devuelve esas violencias a su escala humana -la de los cuerpos concretos sobre los que se ejerce el poder-, creando situaciones de una crudeza difícil de ignorar."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Regina-Jose-Galindo-Museo-del-Chopo-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Vista de la exposición Los peores tiempos posibles , de Regina José Galindo. Museo del Chopo, Ciudad de México, 2026. Foto: Ramiro Chaves", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Los peores tiempos posibles , su actual muestra en el Museo del Chopo , revisa casi tres décadas de esta trayectoria, desde 1999 hasta la actualidad, a través de 33 obras asociadas a distintas temporalidades. La guerra, el genocidio, la migración, el racismo y la experiencia de ser mujer son las condiciones históricas y políticas que organizan el recorrido.", "links": [{"text": "Museo del Chopo", "url": "https://www.chopo.unam.mx/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sin responder a una secuencia cronológica, la curaduría de Maya Juracán y Regina de Con Cossío propone una lectura en la que los acontecimientos del pasado permanecen activos en el presente, y donde las experiencias de violencia de distintos espacios geográficos pueden reconocerse como parte de una misma trama de relaciones de poder."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La noción de tiempo planteada por las curadoras se manifiesta en la reiteración de gestos y en la persistencia del trauma, las huellas de la violencia o de lo que nunca termina de resolverse. Las historias del pasado reaparecen encarnadas en el cuerpo de la artista, en las estructuras institucionales que cuestiona, y en las relaciones geopolíticas que siguen determinando quiénes pueden vivir y en qué condiciones."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Regina-Jose-Galindo-Museo-del-Chopo-4.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Maquillando la muerte (2026). Vista de la exposición Los peores tiempos posibles , de Regina José Galindo. Museo del Chopo, Ciudad de México, 2026. Foto: Ramiro Chaves", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Regina-Jose-Galindo.-El-Chopo.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Maquillando la muerte (2026). Vista de la exposición Los peores tiempos posibles , de Regina José Galindo. Museo del Chopo, Ciudad de México, 2026. Foto: Ramiro Chaves", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Regina-Jose-Galindo-Museo-del-Chopo-9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Vista de la exposición Los peores tiempos posibles , de Regina José Galindo. Museo del Chopo, Ciudad de México, 2026. Foto: Ramiro Chaves", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Estos principios rectores de la obra de Regina José Galindo se expresan con claridad en Maquillando la muerte (2026), una performance realizada durante la inauguración de la exposición. Acostada sobre una camilla, Galindo permanece inmóvil mientras una tanatoesteticista profesional interviene su rostro con productos químicos utilizados en la preparación de cadáveres. La operación se repite diez veces, en alusión al número de mujeres asesinadas diariamente por razones de género en México .", "links": [{"text": "Regina José Galindo", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/?s=regina+jos%C3%A9+Galindo"}, {"text": "número de mujeres asesinadas diariamente por razones de género en México", "url": "https://mexico.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2022-12/infografias%202022_feminicidio.pdf"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La acción parte de una investigación sobre la profesionalización y la expansión de la industria funeraria en un país donde la violencia ha generado una economía especializada en el tratamiento de la muerte. El maquillaje, asociado habitualmente al embellecimiento del rostro, adquiere aquí la función radicalmente distinta de preparar un cuerpo vivo como si ya estuviera muerto. La repetición del procedimiento transforma un gesto técnico en una imagen de la normalización de la violencia feminicida y establece, al mismo tiempo, un vínculo entre las experiencias de Guatemala y México."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "En Línea de autopsia hecha con cocaína contaminada con fentanilo (2025), la artista vuelve a recurrir a la iconografía forense. Una fotografía la muestra desnuda, boca arriba, con la forma de la incisión quirúrgica característica de la autopsia dibujada sobre el torso mediante cocaína contaminada con fentanilo. La imagen condensa las consecuencias de los mercados ilícitos de drogas y las economías de violencia que los acompañan. El cuerpo yace anticipadamente dispuesto para la disección, como si la muerte fuera el desenlace prescrito en la cadena de producción y consumo que opera a escala transnacional."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Galil-regina-jose-galindo.-cortesia-proyectos-ultravioleta.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Regina José Galindo, Galil , 2026. Registro de la performance en Proyectos Ultravioleta, Guatemala. Cortesía de la galería", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La violencia geopolítica propia de las operaciones de limpieza étnica ocupa un lugar central en Galil (2026). En la fotografía que documenta la acción, Galindo yace desnuda, con la boca abierta y municiones de un fusil Galil israelí entre los dientes (y en las manos, a lo largo de la perfomance). El título remite al armamento utilizado por el ejército guatemalteco durante el conflicto armado interno, particularmente en el período del genocidio contra la población maya, y empleado también por el ejército israelí en Palestina."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La obra establece así un paralelismo material entre Guatemala y Gaza, dos geografías que comparten políticas de exterminio. Durante las décadas de 1970 y 1980, Israel suministró armamento, entrenamiento y asesoría militar al Estado guatemalteco, contribuyendo al fortalecimiento de su aparato contrainsurgente. La circulación internacional de estas tecnologías de muerte permite a Galindo señalar la continuidad de las alianzas políticas y militares que hacen posible la violencia contra poblaciones civiles."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La boca llena de municiones evoca el silenciamiento de las víctimas, pero también la voz que persiste en denunciar y resistir. Galil propone así una lectura transhistórica de la destrucción, en la que las fronteras geográficas no impiden reconocer las conexiones entre los sistemas de represión y las potencias que los abastecen."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Regina-Jose-Galindo-Homenaje-a-Latinoamerica-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Regina José Galindo, Homenaje a Latinoamérica (Veladura) , 2026. Fondazione Emilio Scanavino, Milán. Cortesía de la artista", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Regina-Jose-Galindo-Homenaje-a-Latinoamerica-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Regina José Galindo, Homenaje a Latinoamérica (Veladura) , 2026. Fondazione Emilio Scanavino, Milán. Cortesía de la artista", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "El historial de intervenciones estadounidenses en América Latina durante la segunda mitad del siglo XX aparece en Homenaje a Latinoamérica (Veladura) (2026). En esta acción, Galindo yace bajo una tela impregnada con sangre humana de mujeres y hombres latinoamericanos, evocando la imagen de las esculturas clásicas cuyos cuerpos parecen cubiertos por un velo."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La obra responde a Homenaje a Latinoamérica , realizada por los artistas italianos Scanavino y Cavaliere para la XI Bienal de São Paulo de 1971, que reunía los nombres de 162 hombres asesinados por las dictaduras militares latinoamericanas respaldadas por Estados Unidos. A partir de esta referencia, Galindo recupera también la participación de las mujeres en los movimientos revolucionarios y en las luchas políticas de la región. article_text:
A través de 33 obras realizadas desde 1999, la artista guatemalteca Regina José Galindo explora las huellas de la guerra, el genocidio, el racismo y la violencia patriarcal, utilizando su cuerpo como soporte de inscripción de la violencia y como instrumento de denuncia. La exposición, que se podrá ver hasta el 15 de noviembre en el Museo del Chopo de la Ciudad de México, conecta distintas geografías y temporalidades para mostrar cómo las estructuras de dominación siguen operando sobre los cuerpos y la memoria colectiva.

El cuerpo ha sido, desde sus primeras acciones a finales de los años noventa, el principal medio de denuncia e intervención política de Regina José Galindo (Ciudad de Guatemala, 1974). A través de la performance, la artista confronta las estructuras de poder y las formas de violencia que impactan la experiencia individual y colectiva: la represión estatal, el racismo, el colonialismo, el patriarcado y la guerra.

Su práctica se ha desarrollado en relación estrecha con la historia reciente de Guatemala, marcada por el conflicto armado interno (1960-1996) y el genocidio contra la población maya, pero sus preocupaciones desbordan las fronteras nacionales para establecer conexiones con otras geografías y contextos violentos.

En sus acciones, el cuerpo funge como soporte y vehículo de una memoria que no pertenece únicamente a quien la encarna. Galindo lo expone a situaciones de vulnerabilidad, sometimiento y riesgo para hacer visibles mecanismos de dominación que, con frecuencia, permanecen naturalizados o se expresan a través de discursos políticos, cifras y abstracciones. El carácter físico de sus performances devuelve esas violencias a su escala humana -la de los cuerpos concretos sobre los que se ejerce el poder-, creando situaciones de una crudeza difícil de ignorar.

Los peores tiempos posibles , su actual muestra en el Museo del Chopo , revisa casi tres décadas de esta trayectoria, desde 1999 hasta la actualidad, a través de 33 obras asociadas a distintas temporalidades. La guerra, el genocidio, la migración, el racismo y la experiencia de ser mujer son las condiciones históricas y políticas que organizan el recorrido.

Sin responder a una secuencia cronológica, la curaduría de Maya Juracán y Regina de Con Cossío propone una lectura en la que los acontecimientos del pasado permanecen activos en el presente, y donde las experiencias de violencia de distintos espacios geográficos pueden reconocerse como parte de una misma trama de relaciones de poder.

La noción de tiempo planteada por las curadoras se manifiesta en la reiteración de gestos y en la persistencia del trauma, las huellas de la violencia o de lo que nunca termina de resolverse. Las historias del pasado reaparecen encarnadas en el cuerpo de la artista, en las estructuras institucionales que cuestiona, y en las relaciones geopolíticas que siguen determinando quiénes pueden vivir y en qué condiciones.

Estos principios rectores de la obra de Regina José Galindo se expresan con claridad en Maquillando la muerte (2026), una performance realizada durante la inauguración de la exposición. Acostada sobre una camilla, Galindo permanece inmóvil mientras una tanatoesteticista profesional interviene su rostro con productos químicos utilizados en la preparación de cadáveres. La operación se repite diez veces, en alusión al número de mujeres asesinadas diariamente por razones de género en México .

La acción parte de una investigación sobre la profesionalización y la expansión de la industria funeraria en un país donde la violencia ha generado una economía especializada en el tratamiento de la muerte. El maquillaje, asociado habitualmente al embellecimiento del rostro, adquiere aquí la función radicalmente distinta de preparar un cuerpo vivo como si ya estuviera muerto. La repetición del procedimiento transforma un gesto técnico en una imagen de la normalización de la violencia feminicida y establece, al mismo tiempo, un vínculo entre las experiencias de Guatemala y México.

En Línea de autopsia hecha con cocaína contaminada con fentanilo (2025), la artista vuelve a recurrir a la iconografía forense. Una fotografía la muestra desnuda, boca arriba, con la forma de la incisión quirúrgica característica de la autopsia dibujada sobre el torso mediante cocaína contaminada con fentanilo. La imagen condensa las consecuencias de los mercados ilícitos de drogas y las economías de violencia que los acompañan. El cuerpo yace anticipadamente dispuesto para la disección, como si la muerte fuera el desenlace prescrito en la cadena de producción y consumo que opera a escala transnacional.

La violencia geopolítica propia de las operaciones de limpieza étnica ocupa un lugar central en Galil (2026). En la fotografía que documenta la acción, Galindo yace desnuda, con la boca abierta y municiones de un fusil Galil israelí entre los dientes (y en las manos, a lo largo de la perfomance). El título remite al armamento utilizado por el ejército guatemalteco durante el conflicto armado interno, particularmente en el período del genocidio contra la población maya, y empleado también por el ejército israelí en Palestina.

La obra establece así un paralelismo material entre Guatemala y Gaza, dos geografías que comparten políticas de exterminio. Durante las décadas de 1970 y 1980, Israel suministró armamento, entrenamiento y asesoría militar al Estado guatemalteco, contribuyendo al fortalecimiento de su aparato contrainsurgente. La circulación internacional de estas tecnologías de muerte permite a Galindo señalar la continuidad de las alianzas políticas y militares que hacen posible la violencia contra poblaciones civiles.

La boca llena de municiones evoca el silenciamiento de las víctimas, pero también la voz que persiste en denunciar y resistir. Galil propone así una lectura transhistórica de la destrucción, en la que las fronteras geográficas no impiden reconocer las conexiones entre los sistemas de represión y las potencias que los abastecen.

El historial de intervenciones estadounidenses en América Latina durante la segunda mitad del siglo XX aparece en Homenaje a Latinoamérica (Veladura) (2026). En esta acción, Galindo yace bajo una tela impregnada con sangre humana de mujeres y hombres latinoamericanos, evocando la imagen de las esculturas clásicas cuyos cuerpos parecen cubiertos por un velo.

La obra responde a Homenaje a Latinoamérica , realizada por los artistas italianos Scanavino y Cavaliere para la XI Bienal de São Paulo de 1971, que reunía los nombres de 162 hombres asesinados por las dictaduras militares latinoamericanas respaldadas por Estados Unidos. A partir de esta referencia, Galindo recupera también la participación de las mujeres en los movimientos revolucionarios y en las luchas políticas de la región. La sangre convierte el homenaje en una presencia física de las vidas sacrificadas, mientras el cuerpo cubierto de la artista remite a una historia de violencia e intervencionismo cuyas consecuencias siguen vigentes.

La persistencia de las relaciones coloniales y sus formas contemporáneas de explotación también se manifiesta en La conquista (2009), un par de esculturas hechas con cabello de mujeres guatemaltecas para evidenciar su transformación en mercancía dentro de los circuitos comerciales globales. El cabello, central en la identidad personal y en expresiones culturales, pasa a ser un recurso extraído de determinados cuerpos para alimentar una industria que obtiene beneficios de su comercialización.

La conquista y sus herencias culturales son también abordadas en El Conquistador , una performance en la que Galindo permanece dentro de una caja de madera que recuerda un ataúd, mientras un bailaor flamenco ejecuta un zapateado sobre ella durante treinta minutos. La acción sitúa el cuerpo bajo el peso literal y simbólico de una tradición asociada a la cultura española, lo que pone de manifiesto la jerarquía entre quien ejerce la fuerza y quien es dominado por esta.

Las obras reunidas en Los peores tiempos posibles plantean la violencia como una estructura que persiste, se adapta y encuentra nuevos cuerpos sobre los cuales operar. La insistencia de Regina José Galindo en hacer visible lo que se intenta borrar constituye, en este recorrido, una forma de confrontar la historia y las condiciones bajo las cuales se construye la memoria colectiva.

article_text:
Come ogni anno, il Public Program di Art Basel Paris ha portato l’arte contemporanea fuori dagli spazi della fiera, disseminando sculture e installazioni in vari luoghi della capitale francese, più noti e meno noti, tra giardini, piazze e istituzioni storiche. Il programma, gratuito e aperto al pubblico, avrebbe dovuto proseguire fino a domenica 25 ottobre, ma la chiusura anticipata di Art Basel Paris per ragioni di sicurezza legate ai rischi delle manifestazioni , modifica il calendario del weekend: le giornate del 24 e 25 ottobre sono cancellate, e con queste alcune opere del programma pubblico saranno smontate prima del previsto.

Da Tracey Emin a Simone Leigh, da Kutluğ Ataman a Niki de Saint Phalle. Il programma, sostenuto da Miu Miu come Official Partner, riunisce artisti di generazioni e linguaggi diversi, mettendo in dialogo le loro opere con alcuni dei luoghi più significativi di Parigi. Ripercorriamo gli interventi che hanno animato la città e quelli che avremmo potuto incontrare ancora nel corso del weekend.

Il Geste de Consolation di Alice Diop al Palais d’Iéna

Miu Miu presenta al Palais d’Iéna, sede del Consiglio economico, sociale e ambientale (CESE), Geste de Consolation , progetto multidisciplinare della regista francese Alice Diop. Si tratta di uno spazio narrativo che riunisce film, fotografia, scultura, poesia, danza, musica e performance in un montaggio di relazioni ed emozioni. «Voglio che la mia curatela si concentri su gesti di consolazione ideati da artiste nere, ciascuna attiva nella propria disciplina, per riparare lo sguardo feticizzante in cui secoli di storia dell’arte ci hanno confinate», dice Diop.

In Geste de Consolation riunisce donne che «mi hanno guarita, mi hanno nutrita». L’itinerario comprende contributi di Zanele Muholi e Mary Lee Bendolph, un’installazione video di Alice Diop, letture di Penda Diouf, Zora Neale Hurston, June Jordan, Audre Lorde, Marie NDiaye e Zadie Smith e performance di Nadia Beugré, Angel Bat Dawid e Sistazz of the Nitty-Gritty, fino a culminare nella scultura di Simone Leigh, Sentinel (Mami Wata) . Diop concepisce il progetto come un montaggio: il percorso guidato passa da uno spazio all’altro come uno stacco da un’inquadratura alla successiva.

Le sculture monumentali di Tracey Emin

In collaborazione con la Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine, Art Basel Paris e la galleria White Cube presentano tre monumentali sculture in bronzo di Tracey Emin sul tema del corpo femminile. Le opere sono collocate sul Parvis des Droits de l’Homme, nel cuore del Palais de Chaillot. In I lay here for you (2018), una figura prona e allungata oscilla tra esposizione e ritrazione, e la sua superficie tattile restituisce intimità, desiderio e fragilità. In I Followed You to the End (2024) il corpo si solleva in posizione inginocchiata, con le gambe divaricate in un gesto ambiguo, tra tenero invito e brutale sottomissione. I Will Not Be Alone (2025) mostra infine una figura seduta su una roccia: il volto velato porta l’opera oltre il ritratto e la trasforma in un’incarnazione collettiva di forza e resistenza, in cui amore e legame emergono non come sentimenti, ma come condizioni necessarie contro l’isolamento. Nel loro insieme, le tre sculture compongono un percorso dal corpo prono a quello inginocchiato fino a quello seduto, che segna il passaggio dalla resa a una resilienza ostinata.

Kennedy Yanko alla Galerie des moulages

Ancora un progetto del Public Program di Art Basel Paris 2026: nella Galerie des moulages, Kennedy Yanko presenta una nuova serie di sculture in dialogo con i calchi della Galerie Carlu. Utilizzando materiali di recupero, soprattutto metallo, l’artista realizza strutture irregolari rivestite da grandi «pelli» flessibili di vernice acrilica, che vengono colate sul pavimento, fatte asciugare e tagliate prima di essere assemblate con le forme metalliche. Le opere si confrontano così con i capolavori della scultura monumentale francese.

I quaranta schermi di Kutluğ Ataman

La Chapelle des Petits-Augustins des Beaux-Arts ospita Küba (2004), videoinstallazione a quaranta schermi dell’artista Kutluğ Ataman presentata per il Public Program dalla galleria Niru Ratnam di Londra. I televisori sono disposti tra poltrone spaiate e mobili recuperati e raccolgono le testimonianze di quaranta abitanti di Küba, ex insediamento della periferia di Istanbul fondato alla fine degli anni Sessanta da persone in fuga dalle persecuzioni politiche. Ciascuno si rivolge direttamente alla telecamera, raccontando ricordi, credenze, paure e aspirazioni: le storie si sovrappongono e compongono il ritratto collettivo di una comunità segnata da migrazione, povertà e protezione reciproca per la sopravvivenza.

Cosima von Bonin al Petit Palais

Al Petit Palais, Dollys & Beaux (2026) di Cosima von Bonin, presentata da Petzel, Gaga e Neu, ha proposto per il Public Program il suo inconfondibile lessico di creature marine e cani di peluche. L’esposizione è concepita come una mise-en-scène che invita il pubblico a muoversi tra le sculture, interfacciandosi con loro come in uno spazio coabitato piuttosto che considerandole oggetti distanti. Il luogo è popolato da un san Bernardo, una coppia di capesante, un bulldog, un polpo, una balena e alcuni paguri. Da decenni, creature marine e animali domestici popolano la ricerca dell’artista: sono sculture morbide e antropomorfe, sospese ambiguamente tra oggetto decorativo, peluche per bambini e soggetto dotato di agency.

Boz Deseo Garden nel Jardin de la Nouvelle-France

Proseguendo il percorso del Public Program di Art Basel Paris 2026, è significativa anche l’opera di Boz Deseo Garden, Celia, or the Misfortunes of Virtue (2026), presentata da Petrine e installata nel Jardin de la Nouvelle-France. Si tratta di due sculture in acciaio, alte e strette, collocate lungo uno dei sentieri del parco. Le opere sono modellate su un parafulmine trascinato dalle correnti sulle coste del Canale di Bristol, un tempo importante rotta della tratta transatlantica degli schiavi e luogo in cui, negli anni Novanta, fu scoperta una nave negriera affondata. Il Jardin de la Nouvelle-France porta nel suo nome la storia del colonialismo e l’intervento dell’artista vi aggiunge un ulteriore livello di complessità, proseguendo la sua ricerca su come l’eredità della schiavitù plasmi i sistemi di rappresentazione, la memoria e lo spazio pubblico.

Le installazioni monumentali su Avenue Winston Churchill

Avenue Winston Churchill ospita una sequenza di sculture e installazioni di grande formato nello spazio pubblico, sparse tra il Petit Palais e il Grand Palais. Una delle tappe imprescindibili del Public Program. I progetti si interrogano su trasformazione, memoria, vita urbana, identità culturale e rapporto mutevole tra monumentalità e fragilità. Tra le opere, sulla via, anche il CIEL (2026) di Marcello Maloberti , portata dall’italiana Galleria Raffaella Cortese: u n’insegna al neon con la scritta «CIEL» (in francese, «cielo») sospesa a 20 metri d’altezza, sorretta dal braccio esteso di una piattaforma elevatrice. La parola è scritta a mano dall’artista Marcello Maloberti, che spesso realizza grandi opere temporanee nello spazio pubblico per creare momenti di spettacolarità. La scritta è però capovolta, come se fosse destinata a essere letta dal cielo anziché da chi si trova a guardarla dal basso.

E ancora, sempre su Avenue Winston Churchill: Yinka Shonibare , Abstract Bronze VIII (2026), Simone Fattal , Door (2024); Niki de Saint Phalle , Cat Head Totem (2000); Manfred Pernice , bank-group (2026); Alicja Kwade , L’Élévation des Mondes (2026); Carmen Herrera , Angulo Amarillo (2017) e Keita Miyazaki , A Symbiotic Form (2025).

Le opere di Robert Indiana e Lionel Sabatté

Square Jean Perrin: Champs d’Oiseaux (2026) di Lionel Sabatté è presentata dalla galleria Ceysson & Bénétière, raffigura un gruppo di uccelli di bronzo posati su alte colonne, come fermi per una sosta nel mezzo della migrazione, in un fragile equilibrio tra immobilità e movimento, terra e cielo. Lionel Sabatté, finalista del Prix Marcel Duchamp 2025, è noto per l’uso di materiali come polvere, metallo e pietra vulcanica e per opere che indagano la trasformazione dei viventi nel tempo; gli uccelli, discendenti dei dinosauri e testimoni di un’antica storia evolutiva, ricorrono in tutta la sua ricerca.

A Place Clemenceau, Robert Indiana presenta LOVE Wall , portata dalla galleria Almine Rech: una scultura in acciaio Cor-Ten composta da quattro scritte LOVE sovrapposte, due dritte e due capovolte, che trasforma una delle immagini più riconoscibili dell’artista in un’architettura osservabile da più prospettive.

Community

Art Problems: Do I Need an Agent?

Artist agents are not the panacea we imagine them to be, but AI agents won’t solve all your problems, either. Paddy Johnson breaks it down.

Hyperallergic )

My career has stalled, and I spend more time on studio admin than actually working in it. I keep hearing about artist agents. I also keep hearing about AI agents that can do a lot of the administration for you. Do I need an agent or an agent? —Double Agent

I don’t know how much time you spend in the studio versus doing studio administration, but it sounds like the balance is off. The average artist should spend about 30 to 50% of their time on studio administration, depending on how they participate in the industry. And by studio administration, I mean the nuts-and-bolts stuff: inventory management, grant and residency applications, website maintenance. There are exceptions, and most artists will have stretches where admin takes over and vice versa. That’s normal. But the majority of your time shouldn’t be spent on administration. So, let’s get to fixing that.

First order of business: Artist agents are not the panacea we imagine them to be, assuming we can even agree on what they do. The term covers everything from estate planning to brand deals to career strategy. Few of them will write your applications or keep your inventory up to date. Fewer still place artists with galleries. Those agents are a bit like the narwhal, whose tusks were sold as unicorn horns in medieval Europe; the real thing exists, but it rarely lives up to the legend. It may be a spouse who runs the studio, or in one case I know of, a former gallerist placing artists who didn’t speak English at blue-chip galleries. The gallerist took 20% of sales, half from the artist and half from the gallery. It’s an expensive arrangement and it depended on the artists already having a market.

You keep hearing about these roles, though, because the market has had a few rough years. Sales by contemporary art dealers were stagnant in 2025, according to the Art Basel UBS Art Market Report . “Galleries are having to make thoughtful decisions about how they allocate their resources, and many can't carry the staff they once did,” consultant Kristen Becker of KB Art Strategies told me in a recent conversation. Becker offers strategic advice to galleries, nonprofits, artists, and art sponsors. “That means they can't always offer artists the level of support they used to, so we're seeing a range of services, including artist agents, step in to fill that gap.”
