article_text:
Two Emirati filmmakers are bringing distinctly local stories to the 13th edition of the Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth, with Khalid Al Mahmood ’s musical “The Mangrove House” and Abdulrahman Al Madani ’s family drama “Oug,” the only Emirati films in competition.

Both filmmakers have longstanding ties to SIFF. “The Mangrove House,” which world premiered as the festival’s opening film, was pitched at SIFF’s inaugural Film Pitching Session last year as Al Mahmood was seeking post-production support. FANN – Media Discovery Platform, SIFF’s parent organization, subsequently came aboard to back the film. For Al Madani, “Oug” marks the third film he has screened at the festival, following “Nagafa,” which played at SIFF in 2015, and “Laymoon” in 2019.

Related Stories

‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!'

‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’

Their return comes as Emirati filmmakers see renewed momentum around a local industry that has weathered significant ups and downs over the past two decades.

Al Mahmood, who made his first film while a university student in the U.S. in 1999, recalls returning to a UAE where filmmaking was virtually nonexistent, just as an early community of filmmakers was beginning to take shape. Annual screenings of locally made films, which later took shape as the Emirates Film Competition, became “a school where we came together and critiqued our films,” he explains. “More and more festivals popped up,” including the Dubai Intl. Film Festival and Abu Dhabi Film Festival.

Al Madani entered the industry shortly before much of that festival ecosystem disappeared and remembers the “privilege” of having an abundance of platforms before “the plug was pulled, and then we didn’t know where to go next.” Abu Dhabi Film Festival remains defunct, while Dubai, which held its last edition in 2017, is set to return in December 2027.

The loss pushed Al Madani and many Emirati filmmakers of his generation beyond the UAE. In the decade that followed, he made shorts that traveled internationally, an experience he describes as a “wake-up call” that taught him not to solely rely on platforms at home.

Institutional support across the emirates is now growing. “Oug” received a grant from the UAE Ministry of Culture, a significant shift from a period Al Madani describes as having virtually “zero support.”

“We have a long way to go, but I think this is a good start,” he acknowledges. “People feel like they can go and apply somewhere [local] to get funding.”

For Al Mahmood, however, much of the UAE’s film infrastructure remains geared toward attracting international productions rather than sustaining local filmmakers. “What’s missing to me is just the infrastructure to be able to make films in the country,” he argues.

Distribution presents another challenge. This year Al Madani launched Meylas Aflam, a screening initiative aimed at giving Emirati shorts a life beyond their initial festival runs.

“We screen our film once, then what?” he asks. Meylas Aflam has held four sold-out screenings this year, with local audiences staying for discussions that have run as long as an hour.

The response challenges what Al Madani calls a “misconception that our audience is not prepared for our stories.” His films on YouTube have drawn millions of views, he adds, with viewers responding to stories from their own environment “told truthfully, and without sugarcoating.”

‘The Mangrove House’ Al Mahmood’s “The Mangrove House” is a musical about two deaf brothers and their sister trying to raise money for a competition. The project originated with Emirati writer and editor Ayesha Alameri, whose brother is deaf and whose family uses sign language at home.

Al Mahmood admits that when Alameri first brought him the screenplay, he expected the kind of story about living with a disability he had seen before. “Usually the stories are all sad, and it’s going to be a sob story,” he recalls. Instead, what appealed to him was precisely what the screenplay avoided. “There’s no pity. I didn’t feel like they were anything less than any other character.”

That approach grew out of Alameri’s own conversations with her brother. When the two watched films and videos featuring deaf characters, she remembers him asking why their stories “always have to be sad.”

Alameri’s original screenplay ran 23 pages, leaving Al Mahmood with a story he felt was too long to produce affordably as a short but not developed enough for a feature. He concentrated the film around one section of the script and then proposed another departure from its original form, asking, “Why not? Let’s do a musical.”

That decision also gave Al Mahmood an opportunity to root the film more firmly in the UAE, weaving local instruments, clothing and even songs playing with the names of different fish into the story.

“I always felt like I need to introduce something from this part of the world, something that’s rooted here,” he explains. “If it’s not the landscape, it’s the clothing, something.”

‘Oug’ Al Madani draws “Oug” from experiences around him. The title translates as “the defect,” referring to the blame directed at women whose marriages have yet to produce children. The idea grew out of conversations with married women he knew who faced intrusive questions about when they would have children, including a relative who undertook diets, exercise and other measures.

“I was telling her, what about your husband? Does he have to do anything?” Al Madani recalls. “So this question stuck.”

Set largely during a shopping trip to IKEA, the film follows a couple (Sarra’a Abdulaziz, Yaser Al Neyadi) as those pressures surface in a confrontation with the husband’s mother (Huda Al Ghanem). “I wanted it to be completely in a public setting,” Al Madani explains. “They are fighting, but they have to remain composed also. So I felt like it makes it much stronger.”

He also resisted reducing the mother-in-law to a straightforward villain, instead portraying a family in which each character is responding to different expectations. That includes the husband, whose vulnerability culminates in an emotional breakdown.

When Al Madani filmed the scene, he recalls crew members reacting to the sight of an Emirati man in kandura and ghutra, traditional clothing, crying onscreen. “I didn’t realize I was doing a thing,” he admits. “I was just staying true to the story.”

The film’s international run has produced other unexpected reactions. At Denmark’s Odense Film Festival, where “Oug” premiered last year, Al Madani remembers audience members expressing surprise that its hijab-wearing women were the dominant personalities rather than passive figures.

“I was not trying to break stereotypes,” he stresses. “I’m just portraying the truth of my environment, and somehow that broke so many stereotypes.”

For both filmmakers, the next challenge is moving beyond shorts. Al Mahmood has an early-stage feature project he describes only as “very artistic,” while Al Madani has spent the past year developing a feature screenplay and identifies funding as the principal obstacle to making that transition.

“This is my seventh short film. So I am ready,” Al Madani says. “My next project has to be a feature.”

He argues that he is hardly alone.

“There’s a community of filmmakers who have done countless short films,” he adds, “and we need to move on to the next step.”

title_original: Anna Munk’s Cosmetic Still Lifes
editorial_title_zh: 安娜·蒙克的美妆静物画
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位艺术家的最新作品揭示了我们将艺术与青春同等视为受追捧的商品形式。

Munk）的个展《Ombres》来看，用化妆品画脸与画画布并无太大区别。两者都是一种障眼法，根植于修容、高光、阴影——这些都是强调与伪装的技术。曾经，油画颜料本身就是一种戏剧油彩，后来因为有毒才被弃用。蒙克现年三十岁出头，于2022年毕业于哥本哈根丹麦皇家美术学院，她显然对化妆品行业与纯艺术行业之间奇妙的重叠部分深有研究，将有色唇彩、过期的口红、粉底等与她的颜料、色粉、兔皮胶和蜡混合在一起。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "化妆品的材质和色调为她对古典绘画母题的演绎增添了一层闪烁的概念性维度。在这里，七幅静物画的调色板直接取自香奈儿（Chanel）的 Ombres 眼影，有时这些眼影也会与蒙克的颜料融为一体，呈现出闪闪发光的效果。这些色调优雅而克制——淡灰、绿色和裸色、红木色与午夜蓝——并在其静物主题上投射出一种忧郁的氛围和抚慰人心的光泽。斑驳的蜡点让人联想到化妆定妆喷雾——既巩固了下方的底子，又延长了细腻表面的寿命。与此同时，她的母题源自博物馆数字档案中历史静物画的照片。华丽的盘子和玻璃器皿、食物以及死去的家禽等图像被挑选出来、放大，并在其新绘制的空白背景中被孤立地重新构图；蒙克将这些主题视为可供操纵的现成品。颜料和化妆品也可以被视为现成品——两者都是便携的便利品，让我们能够随时随地进行“绘画”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/WEB-AM_Clair-Obscur_a-copy-1230x918.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Clair-Obscur ，2026年，布面油画与蜡，128 "在绘画、数字图像和（再次）绘画之间来回切换，增添了这些作品作为物体描绘和物体本身的观念趣味。人们可能会纳闷，为什么蒙克不直接去观察原作，但从数字源头创作的结果在于，通过屏幕的伪装，光线和材质会产生不同的效果，这使得蒙克的作品恰好能够抵御相机的捕捉——这是对我们这个Instagram友好型绘画时代的解毒剂。在其最初的语境中，静物母题既是财富和繁荣的象征，也是对生命短暂和尘世物体不可避免地衰败的提醒。这与通过化妆品来保持青春有着明显的重合之处。蜡本身就与死亡有着联系，传统上被用于制作死亡面具和木乃伊化。然而，蒙克对静物画的处理似乎并不那么关心浮华（vanitas），而是更关注产品的呈现——这暗示了绘画和身体作为不同类型的奢侈品而被商品化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就所指的内容而言，在蒙克手中，水果并非表面上在腐烂，而是被保存了下来（《Gris Palet》则在灰色、丁香色、烟灰色和鼠尾草色之间变换，体现了蒙克最近对根据历史和现代火灾图像渲染烟雾的兴趣。在这里真正处于生死边缘的是蒙克自己的绘画，由于与化妆品混合，它面临着随时间推移而发生蜕变的风险。在这里，她将多层概念与触觉材料压缩到静物流派中，揭示了我们将艺术和青春等同为令人艳羡的商品形式，同时温和地暗示了它们共同的不稳定性。", "translated": true}, article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The artist’s latest work exposes our equivalencing of art and youth as coveted forms of commodity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the evidence of Anna Munk’s Ombres , painting faces with cosmetics is not dissimilar to painting canvases. Both are types of trickery, rooted in contouring, highlighting, shading – techniques of emphasis and disguise. At one time, oils were themselves a type of theatrical greasepaint, before they were abandoned for being toxic. Munk, who’s in her early thirties and graduated from Copenhagen’s Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in 2022, is evidently well versed in the curious overlaps between the makeup and fine art industries, mingling tinted lip gloss, expired lipsticks, foundation and more with her paints, pigments, rabbit-skin glue and wax."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The materials and hues of cosmetics add a shimmering conceptual layer to her renditions of classical painting tropes. Here, the colour palettes of seven still lifes are taken directly from Chanel’s Ombres eyeshadows, which at times are also melded with Munk’s paints to glistening effect. The shades are classy and restrained – pale grey, green and nude, mahogany and midnight blue – and cast something of a melancholic atmosphere and tranquillising glaze over their still life subjects. article_text:
The artist’s latest work exposes our equivalencing of art and youth as coveted forms of commodity

On the evidence of Anna Munk’s Ombres , painting faces with cosmetics is not dissimilar to painting canvases. Both are types of trickery, rooted in contouring, highlighting, shading – techniques of emphasis and disguise. At one time, oils were themselves a type of theatrical greasepaint, before they were abandoned for being toxic. Munk, who’s in her early thirties and graduated from Copenhagen’s Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in 2022, is evidently well versed in the curious overlaps between the makeup and fine art industries, mingling tinted lip gloss, expired lipsticks, foundation and more with her paints, pigments, rabbit-skin glue and wax.

The materials and hues of cosmetics add a shimmering conceptual layer to her renditions of classical painting tropes. Here, the colour palettes of seven still lifes are taken directly from Chanel’s Ombres eyeshadows, which at times are also melded with Munk’s paints to glistening effect. The shades are classy and restrained – pale grey, green and nude, mahogany and midnight blue – and cast something of a melancholic atmosphere and tranquillising glaze over their still life subjects. Dappled spots of wax recall a cosmetic setting spray – strengthening the ground below and prolonging the life of the nuanced surface. Her motifs, meanwhile, derive from photographs of historical still life paintings in the digital archives of museums. Images of ornate dishes and glassware, food and deceased fowl are picked out, enlarged and reframed in isolation within their new painted voids; Munk treats these subjects as readymades to be manipulated. Paint and makeup might be seen as readymades too – both portable items of convenience that allow us to ‘paint’ on the go.

The shift back and forth between painting, digital image and (again) painting adds to the conceptual intrigue of these works as depictions of objects and objects in themselves. One might wonder why Munk didn’t just look directly at the original painting, but the result of working from a digital source is in the differing effects of light and material through the guise of a screen, which makes Munk’s renditions fittingly resistant to capture by camera – an antidote to our age of Instagram-friendly painting. In their original context, the still life motifs served as symbols of wealth and prosperity, as well as reminders of the transience of life and inevitable decay of earthly objects. There are evident overlaps with the preservation of youth through cosmetics. Wax has its own associations with mortality, being traditionally used for death masks and mummification. And yet Munk’s treatment of the still life seems less concerned with vanitas than the presentation of products – an allusion to the commodification of painting and the body as different types of luxury.

In terms of what’s being signified, then, in Munk’s hands fruit is not ostensibly rotting, but preserved ( Gris Paris , all works 2026); birds, while still and silenced, have not been violently throttled ( Clair-Obscur ). What remains is the quiet residue of a still life, placed within an ethereal painted realm of few details, in which background and motif are treated with equal reverence. Bois Noir , in its inky black palette, drifts closest to abstraction, while Pilo Palet shifts through shades of grey, lilac, smoke and sage, and speaks to Munk’s recent interest in rendering smoke from images of historic and modern fires. What is actually pressingly on the edge of life and death here is Munk’s painting itself, which is at risk of transformation over time thanks to its mingling with cosmetics. Here she compresses layers of conceptual and tactile material into the still life genre, exposing our equivalencing of art and youth as coveted forms of commodity while gently hinting at their shared instabilities.

Anna Munk: Ombres was on view at Galleri Nicolai Wallner, Copenhagen, 21 August – 26 September

The film opens in theaters on October 23."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is an ode to a past New York City and the films set there. article_text:
Note: This interview was originally published as part of our 2026 Sundance coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 23.

Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is an ode to a past New York City and the films set there. John Turturro plays Harry, an old-school pickpocket who’s become out of step with the modern world around him. As a fourth-generation New Yorker, Segan’s roots in the city run deep, though we’ll have to forgive him for setting up shop in Hollywood. Despite his west coast address, it’s clear the filmmaker has a sincere love and understanding of the city, as well as the colorful characters that call it home.

I spoke with Segan during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival about his favorite New York movies, Ricky Jay, and John Turturro’s dancing.

The Film Stage: What made you want to write this story about an aging pickpocket in New York?

Noah Segan : I have always been drawn to things that are tactile. I’m a collector. I’m a lover of analog things. I love magic. I love the idea of skills. That all guided me. As I’m writing, it constantly leads me into these worlds that people don’t talk about because it’s just not in fashion. So I came to this idea of pickpockets and crime. I’m not a criminal, but I’m looking for things that I can wrap my head around and this was one of them. In terms of New York, and the New York I grew up in—of the ’80s and the ’90s—during which crime was still a big part. It just started to make sense.

Which came first? A New York story or a pickpocket story?

I think the pickpocket bit came first. The idea of, you know, “What is magic in the real world?” This guy is a magician. He’s Ricky Jay. He’s got this incredible ability, and how does that function in reality? And where does that function? The place I know the best.

Noah Segan

How long have you been working on this idea?

About eight years ago, I decided to stay home with our infant daughter when my wife went back to work, as opposed to doing what I’ve been doing for most of my life, which is being what they call a character actor—a guy who takes the gig and goes and does it. We both work in show business, so one of us having a steady gig was enough for me to stay. While I was home with her and she was napping, I was writing the script. I happened to finish it when Rian [Johnson] was gearing up to do the first Knives Out movie. He said, “Hey, man. Come on out and do this.” I showed him the script, and he said, “You know, I think if things go well with this movie, maybe we could start a company and this could be the kind of thing the company could help make.”

What’s it like making a movie in the city these days?

It’s funny. For those of us from New York, whether it was me or John [Turturro] or much of our crew, it felt like an adventure. It felt like, “Well, of course, we’re going to do this, because that’s what people in New York do. They do crazy shit and they kind of get away with it. By the skin of your teeth, we make it happen.” The people who were not from New York were like, “How the hell are we going to do this? What do you do with a subway? Do you rent a subway? What do you mean you sneak on a subway? What do you mean, you just put the camera on the street?” Well, people don’t worry about that. They just go about their business.

What were you looking for in each of those individual locations?

I was looking for something that felt like recognition to me. That was going up to the neighborhood in the Bronx where my grandfather grew up, which is not far from Arthur Avenue, and that scene. Going out to Queens, where my brother lives. Shooting in the part of Brooklyn that I was born in––Prospect Park South, Ocean Avenue. I was looking for places that felt like my home. And then the Staten Island of it all, it’s funny: I spent more time on Staten Island shooting this movie than I did the previous 40 years of my life. But the idea of going over the Verrazano Bridge and having this view of the city that we don’t see that often. Usually we see the city from Jersey, from this other perspective. But from the water on the Staten side of the Verrazano, you really get a picture of the city while being in the city.

What were your references for the film?

There’s so many great “people on the run in New York” movies. As much as I love After Hours and as much as I love the Safdies, a movie that I kept going back to was Desperately Seeking Susan . Another one I always think of as a companion piece to Desperately Seeking Susan is The Linguini Incident . You know, I’m just going to reference Rosanna Arquette movies. Mikey and Nicky is there, but also Nicole Holofcener shows a lot of New York in a really elegant, beautiful way.

And then outside of New York, John and I really connected on a mutual love of Robert Mitchum and how he really embodied a sensitive masculinity. He was never afraid to be gentle while being Robert Mitchum, while being one of the great cops of our day. Out of the Past , The Friends of Eddie Coyle , even though that’s set in Boston. I’ve got a big Friends of Eddie Coyle poster in my house. Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia came up as well, which is another great run-around movie. It’s set in Mexico, but also it’s about a guy who can’t stop moving.

What are some underappreciated movies that are set in New York? Ones that people don’t get out to see often enough.

As a genre man, Ganja & Hess is a great New York movie. It has this off-the-wall genre thing going on.

It is, though it doesn’t feel really like it’s New York either. It has such an otherworldly nature to it.

It’s a fairy tale, right? And yet it is very New York. Across 110th Street was something that came up a lot for us. Hal Hartley and Whit Stillman are very much in this film as well. Movies that may have not been made with huge budgets, but were made very much in New York.

© 2026 Sundance Institute | photo by Jemal Countess

Originally, you wanted John Turturro’s character Harry to be older. Was there someone in particular you had in mind?

The only actor whom I ever thought of very early on, because of the connection to magic, was the late, great Ricky Jay. He obviously was a student of criminology as much as a student of magic, and a great New Yorker. I got to know him shortly before he passed a little bit, so in my mind, I don’t even know if I was thinking of Ricky particularly, or if it was more the concept of Ricky and the specificity of Ricky, because there was only one Ricky.

Then when it came time to cast the movie, I was like, “Well, shit, there’s only one John Turturro.” I never thought that was going to happen. It was one of those things where if we’re gonna make this movie, we’ve got to take a big swing. Why not? Why can’t I win the lottery? We sent it to John and he was like, “Let me have lunch with this guy tomorrow,” thinking that I’m in New York. I was like, “I’m in L.A. Let me hop on this flight tonight.” We had some soup and fell in love.

How much of the hostility toward technology is based in your own struggles or frustrations?

When I became a dad, I was like, “I don’t want to be a fuddy duddy.” I want to be there for my kids, which means having a finger on the pulse and not necessarily being some old-school guy who is only into the analog shit. But I also don’t want to lose what we have. And that means I don’t want to lose the city that we have. I don’t want to lose the objects that we have. Whether it’s the watches or the phones that don’t have the screens on them or the clothing that lasts forever. I don’t think that there are mutual exclusivities, but I do want to protect the things that are real. That’s a big part of what’s happening with film and television right now and with storytelling. How do we protect these things we love?

Tell me about that scene of John dancing to “Native New Yorker.” It’s so joyful and he just seems so into it.

I put that song on a playlist that I shared with John. It was sort of a stream-of-consciousness thing I was doing where I was trying to find music I loved that I thought represented vibes from the movie. And he said, “You know, man, I remember this song. I remember going to nightclubs and dancing to that song.” And John loves to dance. He’s a great dancer; he’s a trained dancer. Very early on in the process, he sent me a video of him in his office dancing to the song. And I swear to God, I could hear his wife downstairs, going, “John, are you dancing to that song again?”

He was just in the groove and I thought, “You know, we’ve got to find that moment.” Because Harry is a guy who starts off looking for a win, and we don’t know the last time he had a win. He’s doing his thing, he’s making ends meet, and I wanted him to have a moment where he had a win. And that win was also a win for John, and it was a win for me and [cinematographer] Sam [Levy]. When we shot that scene, it was just me, Sam on the camera, John dancing in the room, and Karina [Arroyave], who played his wife Rosie. The four of us just got to have a little party, and that’s kind of what the movies are about. It’s a moment in the movie. It’s a real moment in the movie, and a moment for us.

What were some places or aspects of the city you didn’t get a chance to include?

It’s funny: at our kids’ preschool they had a Culture Day. Everybody is supposed to bring something that represents their culture. On the sign-up sheet, somebody had already picked bagels. I thought, “All right, what about hot dogs?” And my wife goes, “What do you mean, hot dogs?” I said, “Well, hot dogs—that’s my culture. It’s, like, New York culture. It’s like bagels. Papaya King, Gray’s Papaya, Nathan’s are New York culture.” My wife, still to this day, makes fun of me. I would have loved to have had Harry having a pineapple champagne and a recession special up on 72nd Street at some point.

You got B&H in there.

We got B&H! We didn’t get Papaya Dog, but we got B&H and that was such a win. The folks who run B&H, Ola, is in the movie, and you can hear Leo in the background chopping it up on the grill. That was so special because, as a punk rock kid who spent a lot of time sneaking into Niagara and going to shows at Coney Island High and making my way down to ABC No Rio, Arlene’s Grocery… Yonah Schimmel’s! Man, I wish we got Yonah Schimmel’s in there—best knish in town. But being able to start the movie at B&H with a plate of matzo brie, I think sets the tone.

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

"“这感觉更像是一种科技公司的解雇方式，而不是传统制片厂的做法。这很耻辱、很糟糕，并且加剧了我们所有人都在按硅谷规则打工的感觉，”该经纪人说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该消息人士指出，具有讽刺意味的是，就在巴贾里亚被解雇的两周前，她在Netflix的前任——辛迪·霍兰德（Cindy Holland）——也刚在Skydance的新岗位上仓促被炒。霍兰德的职位被牺牲掉，是为了给凯西·布洛伊斯（Casey Bloys）腾出空间，这位HBO负责人随着华纳兄弟探索频道（Warner Bros. Discovery）合并的完成，现已全面接管流媒体业务。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Netflix这场轰动的高管大地震，加上业内人士从Netflix本周实施的裁员中解读出的种种信号，再次引发了关于这家流媒体巨头将重新着手收购一家大型制片厂或其他重要内容资产的猜测。鉴于该公司明年将从康卡斯特（Comcast）分拆出来，NBCUniversal（NBC环球）是一个合乎逻辑的目标，因此它将比整个康卡斯特更小、更容易管理。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "转向赖斯也引发了人们的疑问：在巴贾里亚领导下，Netflix是否还会继续保持其激进的本土语言内容战略。萨兰多斯（Sarandos）本周的一份备忘录指出，Netflix需要为“UCAN”市场（他们对美国和加拿大的古怪称呼）推出更多引发热议的热门作品，这并未被忽视。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据多位消息人士透露，巴贾里亚是在周三晚上得知这一残酷现实的。当时她在好莱坞的流媒体办公室里堵住了Netflix联席CEO特德·萨兰多斯，就在洛杉矶一处私人住宅为喜剧《无能为之》（“Nobody Wants This”）第3季首播举行放映会之前。（值得注意的是，在活动流出的任何宣传照片中都没有看到萨兰多斯或巴贾里亚的身影。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巴贾里亚开门见山地向萨兰多斯询问甚嚣尘上的传言是否属实——而据信原本打算在周一公布这一消息的萨兰多斯，当时便将实情告诉了她。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有关巴贾里亚命运的传言在最近几个月里一直甚嚣尘上。随着派拉蒙与华纳兄弟探索频道（Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery）合并大戏的持续推进，坊间有诸多猜测认为HBO负责人布洛伊斯将跳槽到Netflix担任要职，或者为该流媒体平台创立一个资金充足的高端厂牌。但一旦布洛伊斯被证实为Skydance流媒体业务的新掌门人，关于巴贾里亚的猜测便冷却了下来。周一，巴贾里亚还曾亮相戛纳Mipcom内容大会的舞台，并接受了由Variety和Mipcom颁发的表彰其对全球市场贡献的先锋奖（Vanguard Award）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，就在欧洲顶级内容行业内部人士聚集一堂聆听巴贾里亚演讲之际，本周好莱坞关于她未来的讨论再次死灰复燃。事实证明，这是一场完美的风暴：Netflix正严阵以待准备迎接其有史以来规模最大的一次裁员，其第三季度财报也将于10月20日发布。此次裁员占公司员工总数的6%，即约1,000个岗位，于周二和周三执行。这意味着，当周四洛杉矶午餐时间刚过、赖斯上任的重磅消息袭来时，Netflix的员工们早已处在风口浪尖上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时就在两周前，赖斯还向朋友们表示他对重新出任高管毫无兴趣——这表明萨兰多斯在得知赖斯可被争取后迅速采取了行动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据了解，巴贾里亚收到了来自她在国内外创意界广泛人脉的大量支持。多位消息人士称，这位高管直言不讳地告诉朋友们自己感到震惊，这与她一贯的坦率作风相符。巴贾里亚拒绝置评。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "接下来，聚光灯将转向巴贾里亚旗下的两名核心垂直业务副手——负责电影业务的林芝（Dan Lin）和负责原创剧集的金妮·豪（Jinny Howe）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "林芝在Netflix的电影业务部门担任了2年半的稳健掌舵人，他的上任是为了制止该流媒体在早期斯科特·斯图伯（Scott Stuber）时代的大手大脚。然而，削减预算也伴随着情感代价，林芝被迫确保演职人员在没有萨兰多斯那张被普遍认为开出的空白支票的情况下，交付出高质量的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了制作成本更低的电影外，林芝还支持了一些备受瞩目的收购项目（如《艾米莉亚·佩雷斯》以及Netflix目前最有望冲奥的竞争者《La Bola Negra》）。然而，大量报道暗示，随着赖斯掌权，林芝将离开公司。时机再敏感不过了，因为Netflix将于2月份以全面院线上映的形式推出格蕾塔·葛韦格备受期待的《纳尼亚传奇：魔法师的外甥》。就在巴贾里亚被解雇的同时，坊间传闻立刻将刚被免职的华纳兄弟影业负责人迈克尔·德·卢卡（Michael De Luca）和帕梅拉·阿布迪（Pamela Abdy）推为潜在的接替人选（这一传闻其实在一个月前派拉蒙和华纳兄弟探索公司最终找到合并路径时就已开始流传）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据业内人士透露，由于赖斯上任后很可能会将工作重心放在电影方面，美国和加拿大剧本业务负责人豪目前的职位似乎很安全。好莱坞有传言称，Netflix最近在复制《怪奇物语》或《布里奇顿》这样的现象级大热剧集方面举步维艰，而于2025年8月接任的豪手头有着繁重的项目排期，并且才刚刚开始看到她自己的一些开发项目结出硕果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这其中包括主演《纠正》的梅丽尔·斯特里普、主演《兔子，兔子》的亚当·德赖弗和迈克尔·法斯宾德、马丁·斯科塞斯的《罗马人》以及真人/CGI结合的《史酷比：起源》。流媒体业务面临着繁重的剧集储备，而她正开始看到自己主导的开发项目初见成效。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“他们希望她留下来，”一位消息人士说。“如果她走了，那对他们来说将是一场灾难。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，鉴于赖斯的经验，一些人也禁不住好奇，萨兰多斯是否刚刚雇佣了一位最终可能成为取代他的人选——以防公司股价继续下跌且管理层认为需要做出更多变动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这周上演的戏剧性场面，确实比Netflix今年在其平台上推出的任何内容都要精彩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "（图自：彼得·赖斯、贝拉·巴贾里亚、林芝和金妮·豪）", "translated": true}]

article_text:
It started with a dinner.

Peter Rice and Ynon Kreiz met for a meal in late September, days before Kreiz surprised the industry by jumping from the CEO job at Mattel to become co-chief executive of Skydance with David Ellison.

The report of the Kreiz-Rice meeting came in the New York Post’s Page Six after Kreiz’s role at Skydance was announced. That set off speculation that he was recruiting Rice for a big role at the enlarged studio. It turns out Kreiz had been trying to persuade Rice to take a board seat at Barbie’s house.

Related Stories

Sony in Talks to Land 'Battlefield' Video Game Movie From Christopher McQuarrie and Michael B. Jordan

Electronic Arts Laying Off 3% of Employees in Studios Restructuring: BioWare Shutting Down, Respawn and DICE to Team on 'Star Wars: Battlefront 3'

Rice, however, was not destined to advise on matters of Uno and Matchbox cars. The former Fox Searchlight and Fox Networks Group chief — who went to Disney in 2019 as its top TV executive only to be unceremoniously axed during the Chapek regime — has vaulted back to one of the town’s most powerful posts: chief content officer of Netflix .

Popular on Variety

Media coverage of Kreiz’s courtship of Rice is one of the spurs that pushed Netflix to make the move on a hire that will have ripple effects across its expansive film and TV operations. The ouster of Bela Bajaria from the role that Rice now occupies was messy, and angered many inside and outside of Netflix.

“We don’t live in Hollywood right now. We live in Silicon Valley,” said a prominent agent, citing the general mood of the creative community. The brusque treatment of an executive of Bajaria’s stature is a sign that no one is safe from scrutiny, and no one should ever count on making a graceful exit.

LISTEN to Variety’s Matt Donnelly, Cynthia Littleton and Michael Schneider break down the shakeup at Netflix

“It feels like more of a tech approach than a studio approach to letting someone go. It’s shameful, it sucks and it adds to the feeling that we’re all working by Silicon Valley rules,” the agent said.

The source noted the irony of Bajaria getting the ax just two weeks after the executive that she replaced at Netflix — Cindy Holland — was also hastily ousted from her new role at Skydance. Holland’s role was sacrificed to make room for Casey Bloys, the HBO chief who is taking over all streaming now that the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is completed.

The bombshell executive upheaval at Netflix, coupled with signals that insiders are reading from the layoffs that Netflix implemented this week, has set off renewed speculation about the streaming giant getting back in the hunt for a major studio or some other significant content assets. NBCUniversal is a logical target, given that the company will be spun out from Comcast next year and thus would make for a much smaller and more manageable acquisition than the entirety of Comcast.

The switch to Rice also raises questions about whether Netflix will remain as aggressive in its local-language content strategy as it had been under Bajaria. A memo from Sarandos this week saying that Netflix needs to deliver more buzzy hits for the “UCAN” market (their wonky term for the United States and Canada) did not go unnoticed.

Bajaria, according to multiple sources, learned the harsh reality of her fate on Wednesday evening when she cornered Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos at the streamer’s offices in Hollywood, just before the screening at a private residence in L.A. for the Season 3 premiere of comedy “Nobody Wants This.” (Notably, neither Sarandos nor Bajaria are seen in any of the publicity photos that have been shared from the event.)

Bajaria asked Sarandos point-blank whether there was truth to the rumors gaining stream — and Sarandos, who it’s believed was originally going to break the news on Monday, told her at that moment.

Rumors about Bajaria’s fate have swirled in recent months. As the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger saga soldiered on, there was much speculation about HBO chief Bloys jumping ship for a big role at Netflix or to launch a well-funded prestige label for the streamer. But once Bloys was confirmed as the new top boss of streaming for Skydance, the Bajaria speculation cooled off. On Monday, Bajaria was on stage at the Mipcom content conference in Cannes, where she accepted the Vanguard Award for contributions to the global marketplace as bestowed by Variety and Mipcom.

But even as top European content industry insiders gathered to hear Bajaria speak, chatter about her future fired back up in Hollywood this week. It turned out to be a perfect storm of events, with Netflix bracing for its largest-ever layoffs and its third-quarter earnings report coming on Oct. 20. The layoffs, amounting to 6% of the company’s workforce, or about 1,000 positions, were implemented Tuesday and Wednesday. That meant Netflix staffers were already on edge when the shock of the Rice news hit just after lunchtime in L.A. on Thursday.

Meanwhile, as recently as two weeks ago Rice was telling friends that he had no interest in becoming an executive again — which is a sign that Sarandos acted fast as soon as he learned Rice was available.

Bajaria is understood to have received an outpouring of support from her wide network of contacts in the creative community, at home and abroad. Multiple sources say the executive has been telling friends outright that she is shell-shocked, in keeping with her reputation for candor. Bajaria declined to comment.

The microscope now turns to Bajaria’s two top vertical lieutenants — Dan Lin in film, and Jinny Howe in original TV series.

Lin has been a steady hand in Netflix’s film operations for two-and-a-half years, ushered in to stop the lavish spending of the streamer’s formative Scott Stuber era. Slashing budgets carries an emotional price, though, and Lin has been forced to ensure talent delivers quality product without a widely perceived blank check signed by Sarandos.

In addition to making cheaper movies, Lin also backed some high-profile acquisitions (“Emilia Pérez” and Netflix’s current best-hope Oscar contender “La Bola Negra”). Yet, numerous reports have suggested that Lin will exit the company as Rice comes into power. It couldn’t be a more sensitive time, as Netflix will launch Greta Gerwig’s anticipated “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” with a full theatrical release in February. As Bajaria got the boot, the rumor mill instantly offered forth Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy — the ousted Warner Bros. Pictures chiefs — as potential replacements (which actually started a month ago, as Paramount and WBD finally found a path to combine).

According to insiders, with Rice likely to kick off his tenure by focusing on the film side of things, U.S. and Canada scripted head Howe appears to be safe in her role. With whispers in Hollywood that Netflix has struggled recently to produce another megahit in the vein of “Stranger Things” or “Bridgerton,” Howe, who took over in August 2025, has a hefty slate on her plate and is just starting to see some of her own development come to fruition.

That includes Meryl Streep in “The Corrections,” Adam Driver and Michael Fassbender in “Rabbit, Rabbit,” Martin Scorsese’s “The Roman” and the live-action/CGI “Scooby-Doo: Origins.”

“They want her to stay,” said one source. “If she left, that’d be a disaster for them.”

Meanwhile, given Rice’s experience, some also wondered whether Sarandos just hired someone who could ultimately be a candidate to replace him — should the stock continue to suffer and the company see a need to make more changes.

The week has indeed offered more drama than anything Netflix will put on its service this year.
